en: Preface to the *Commentary on the Profound Meaning of the Mahāyāna-śāstra*,
composed by Wen Zhengliang, who assisted in propagating the teachings, shared the same virtue, and contributed to the realization of the principles;
Grand Master with the Rank of State Councilor, Acting Grand Preceptor, concurrently Minister of the Secretariat, Supervisor of National History, and Director of the Bureau of Military Affairs.
Shangzhuguo, Duke of Yan, with a fief of seven thousand five hundred households and a real allotment of one hundred and fifty households,
Your Servant Ye Lü Xiaojie, respectfully composed this by imperial decree. I, your servant,
have heard that when the Awakened Sovereign established his teachings, he initiated the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) to propagate the sublime path and set forth its guiding principles.

The Three Vehicles manifest transformations in accordance with the diverse capacities of sentient beings. As the Sūtras state, they are boundless, extending beyond the limits of heaven and earth and impossible to exhaust;
their Dharma-meaning is profoundly deep, such that even the vast capacity of rivers and seas cannot fathom it.
From the time of its initial compilation until its subsequent dissemination, many years have elapsed; who was able to expand and propagate it? There was a Bodhisattva named Aśvaghoṣa.
With a body that has realized the fruit through the ten bodies, he dwelt in the eighth stage—the ground where causes are manifested—to proclaim the orthodox teaching and refute heterodox schools.
He composed the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* to accord with the verbal teachings of the Tathāgata.

Subsequently, the Great Master Nāgārjuna, looking up to emulate his teacher’s virtue, succeeded him as the presiding leader; relying on the subtle essence of the five divisions of the canon, he fashioned the profound mysteries of ten fascicles.

It is titled the *Śikṣā-mahāyāna-śāstra*. This is the profound exposition of the Dharma that encompasses both the general and the specific through the gates of the Buddha’s birth and other [aspects], and which possesses the esoteric principles of both subject and object.
Since its circulation in China until the time of the translations by Paramārtha, no sage or philosopher has yet encountered it; how, then, could its pure brilliance be revealed?
I, the Heavenly Protected Emperor, occupy the throne as the successor to eight generations;
my virtue surpasses that of a hundred sovereigns,
and my sagely wisdom is renewed daily.
Endowed with vast compassion by nature, he had thoroughly mastered the essential points of governance through a comprehensive study of Confucian classics;

he had also fully exhausted the profound subtleties of the Buddhist scriptures and the wondrous essence of the Dharma-nature school. He once remarked: "The *Śrīmālā-sūtra-śāstra* encompasses the marvels of the One Vehicle."
In summing up the profound portals of a hundred scriptures, how could one not seek a master to compose a commentary on their meaning?

Shi Siguang Quan, the Great Master Yuanjin, whose learning surpassed that of Guanzhi and whose eloquence eclipsed that of Daosheng and Fayong, frequently accompanied the Emperor in palace discussions and deeply fulfilled the imperial intent.
Having recently been requested by the assembly, he has now succeeded in reaching [the throne].

Upon hearing this, His Majesty graciously deigned to issue a decree, commanding that the hidden meanings be extensively sought. Thereupon, I thoroughly cleansed the vessel of wisdom and secretly sharpened the blade of my rhetoric;
having refined my studies for barely ten months, I completed five fascicles analyzing these principles. When I submitted them for imperial review, I was indeed honored by his commendation.
Thereupon, he was granted the title "Zanxuan" (Elucidator of the Mysterious),
as the Emperor, in the intervals between attending to state affairs and during his tours of inspection, examined the work in detail and published it extensively.
Having personally verified this through experience,
I shall first establish my own interpretation of the four paths within this treatise.

Having thoroughly penetrated the teachings of antiquity, he inspires faith in future generations; what the multitude has never heard and the common mind cannot conceive, his genius alone excels, and public acclaim converges upon him.
Like a compass needle amidst a great mist, he points the way; like the myriad stars bowing to the North Star, all things turn toward him.
His meaning encompasses the fifty-one *piṭakas*, which, when investigated, are inexhaustible; his principles are divided into thirty-three aspects, which remain unshakably firm.
The Imperial Edict followed the words of Mo Lou, commissioning the transmission so that this mirror for the eyes might endure forever and shine eternally alongside the stars.

This humble servant reverently receives the gracious decree to assist in compiling these precious records; yet the brilliant Heaven of Meaning is beyond the reach of a tube-spy’s gaze, and the vast Ocean of Learning is but a drop from a ladle.
Having deliberated upon this, fearing it would only cause needless trouble, I have had no leisure for further refinement and have merely set forth the general outline.
This concludes the first volume of the *Commentary on the Praśasti to the Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*.
Preface to the Tenfold Analysis,
Volume Two; following the explanation of the General Body.
Fascicle Three:
The Explanation of the Section on the Arising and Ceasing of the Mind.
Fascicle Four follows below.
The fifth fascicle concludes the section on the "Stage of Abiding in Ignorance" (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*) within the *Śrāvaka-parivarta*,
and continues from the section on the "Great Functioning" (*mahā-vṛtti*) until the end.
Table of Contents for the *Commentary on the Profound Meaning of the Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* (End).
*Commentary on the Profound Meaning of the Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, Scroll One, including the Preface.
Chonglu Da-fu, Acting Minister of Works, Quen Yuan Tong, Bao’en Chuanjiao Temple, Central Capital.
Written by Imperial Decree by the Dharma Master, the Purple-Robed Subject and Śramaṇa Fawu:
The ocean of the perfect and eternal fruition is a profound, tranquil, and numinous source; it is inconceivable beyond the teachings and supreme, transcending causes and conditions.
How could the four dharma realms contain it? How could the three worlds suffice to encompass it? This is the sublime teaching of the Dharma Gate.
Twofold yet utterly transcendent, it is beyond subject and object; profound and silent, it stands alone, beyond all description or causal conditions.

It cannot be known by the intellect, nor is it a number among numbers. That which is truly "numberless" is none other than the non-dual Mahāyāna. Void and serene, it is fundamentally one; radiant and manifest, it accords with conditions.

Whether as the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) or the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), whether arising from the beginning or following from causes, both mundane and supramundane paths ultimately converge in the same destination. This is what is called "Suchness."

The "Treasury of the Wish-Fulfilling Jewel" (Cintāmaṇigarbha) is so named because its applications are inexhaustible; how much more so for the Great Divine King (Mahādeva-rāja), whose majestic spirit is unfathomable!
This refers to the sixteen modes of entry into the Dharma. Therein, the conventional and the ultimate are distinguished, yet the sudden and the gradual are not intermingled.

They are categorized by their respective stages in mutual relation, while their essence and characteristics remain quiescent and transcendent, pure and pristine. Thus, the positions differ according to cause and effect, and wisdom accordingly.

The provisional establishment of delusion within the nature of abandonment and cultivation, and the non-existence of obstacles to the Way within the process of negation and affirmation—this is precisely what is meant by the "sixteen gates of entry.
Therefore, our World-Honored One, following the vehicle he originally mounted, spoke in accordance with the meaning;

yet, since the sudden transformation at the Śāla Grove, the guidance was lost, and the profound depths of the Dragon Treasury (the Tripitaka) remain utterly unfathomable and their hidden mysteries unexplored.

Ming Bodhisattva lamented that these profound principles remained hidden within the traps and snares [of conventional expression], while sentient beings were mired in ignorance regarding cultivation and realization.

Consequently, having completed two *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* of practice, he relied upon the ineffable and, drawing from hundreds of *lakṣa* of scriptures, he composed the *Mahāyāna-śāstra* to fully elucidate the universal Dharma;
this treatise, consisting of no more than ten thousand words, encompasses all essential meanings.
Encompassing all scriptures, it initiates the path of fruition and integrates the gateway of causes;

yet, as the Dharma teachings are profound and vast while the capacities of beings are shallow and limited, they have not yet reached the deep essence of the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). This is like peering at the heavens through a tube:

one may roughly observe the vast expanse, but a single hair-tip cannot fathom the depths of the ocean. The Great Being Nāgārjuna, having received a prophetic prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), emerged [to reveal this truth].
He gave rise to guidance for the dispositions of sentient beings and manifested this as a treatise on the meaning of inclusion, precisely suited to those whose faculties delight in brevity.

Relying upon the golden words of a hundred texts, he extensively explained a single scroll of precious scriptures; masters and disciples followed in succession, their legacy flowing in fragrance through the ages.
Since its translation during the Later Qin period, it has been transmitted through successive generations, yet its widespread dissemination had not yet occurred [at that time].
I have previously heard that what was lost over many ages must surely await its destined opportunity for revival; indeed, we have now encountered external protection and witnessed a true renaissance.
Our Celestial Emperor, the Son of Heaven, descends from the illustrious lineage of the Kṣatriyas and succeeds to the precious heritage of the Cakravartin kings.

While attending to the affairs of state, he relishes the profound winds of the Mysteries; ascending the imperial throne, he discusses the subtle truths, whereby extraordinary auspicious signs flow forth and the Perfect Doctrine is brought to its ultimate fulfillment.

He composed hymns of praise to announce auspicious signs; having thoroughly investigated the various scriptures, he was especially proficient in this treatise, and his realization of the Dharma was received in successive layers.

An imperial edict was issued to the Attendant Lecturer of the Inner Court: "Since you have roughly demonstrated the gateways of meaning, I am fortunate to look up to your realization in accord with the Sage’s intention.
Therefore, I command you to present your most earnest words so that a separate commentary may be composed, in order to further propagate the purport of the treatise.
Upon its arrival, [he]...

Your Sacred Majesty has deigned to bestow these former words; yet, while the transmission of the Lamp and the waving of the fly-whisk are beyond my capacity to praise, how could I dare to presume to take up the brush and ink? I shall strive to fulfill [your command].
I briefly set forth these humble words from the depths of my heart.
I prostrate before the ocean of the perfect nature-virtue, the pure awakening of subject and object, and the Bodhisattva Dharmakara along with all other worthy sages.
I pray that you will grant your secret assistance to aid this profound mystery.
To explain this treatise, there is a tenfold analysis: first, the causes and conditions for its composition; second, the presentation of the structural gates of the teaching;

third, the control and explanation of the grand framework; fourth, the opening of the secret keys for cultivation; fifth, exhortations to uphold and warnings against slandering; sixth, the classification of the teachings according to their meaning;

seventh, the definitive discernment of the essence of the treatise; eighth, the revelation of the fundamental tenets and purport; ninth, the era in which it was propagated; and tenth, the detailed analysis of the text.
Regarding the meaning:
first, the causes and conditions for the initial arising [of the teaching] have both general and specific aspects.

The general refers to all the various sūtras responding to causes and answering requests, and all the various treatises revealing principles and delivering sentient beings; the emergence of the entire body of teachings throughout a lifetime is entirely due to these. The specific...
This means that this treatise, in sum, enumerates eight causes for the subsequent fourfold division;

it establishes three aggregates, enters the five stages, removes obstacles such as doubt, breaks through attachments to a self and so forth, penetrates the two gates, and realizes the unity of the one mind. Thus it is.
Second, regarding the exposition of the methods of the gates, the *Commentary on the Section on Establishing the Meaning* states: "The names and numbers of the dharma-gates total thirty-three.

Because this non-dual Mahāyāna is profound, subtle, and uniquely supreme, its ocean of fruit transcends words and is beyond roots; therefore, the subsequent treatise refers to it as 'intrinsic virtue' (*xingde*)."
The "Perfected Ocean" (Yuanman Hai) refers to the remaining thirty-two, whether as gates or dharmas, all of which belong to the causal portion (*hetubhāga*). Furthermore, the lower treatise states:

"The ocean of the seeds cultivated through practice" refers to these [sixteen]. The two layers of the fundamental "objects entered" (*praveśya*) both belong to the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) and constitute the totality;
the sixteen "means of entry" (*praveśaka*), being the two layers of branches and sub-branches, do not [belong to the ultimate truth].

Since both the ultimate and conventional truths emerge as distinct meanings, the *Vyākhyā* states: "This single general statement serves as the universal essence within two locations, because it looks upward and downward.
It further states: "From beginning to end, the fundamental and the derivative do not become confused;
thus, in the sequence of the general and the specific, there is no lack of standard. Based on what is said here, [the claim that] it is not [the case]... is incorrect.
That the opening of the preceding section serves as the basis for the subsequent treatise on the Dharma is evident;

yet, if one were to find confusion and disorder regarding the primary and secondary aspects, the general and specific categories, and the meaning of the Three Truths within that preceding section, it would truly be a failure of genius to seek out the hidden and of sagely wisdom to explore the profound mysteries. Only by thoroughly investigating the root can one explain its tenets, for only then does one deeply accord with the principles of the general and the specific.
From this point forward, the following is a further expansion of the Imperial Commentary,
which states that because the non-dual Mahāyāna Dharma transcends the faculties of sentient beings and is beyond verbal teaching,

it is without cause or condition, inconceivable and ineffable; yet, although the nature of the Buddha’s perfect oceanic fruition is fundamentally beyond words, it is here explained from the perspective of the causal stage.

Regarding the teaching that the *dharmadhātu* is for the benefit of sentient beings, when analyzed according to its aspects of subject and object, and further distinguished by the differences between sharp and dull faculties, the Dharma is thus divided into two layers.

First, although the Dharma to be entered belongs to the non-dual Great Vehicle of the ocean of fruition (*phala-sāgara*), within the causal stage it is given a provisional name where no name exists, being termed the "Root Great Vehicle. This is discussed in terms of its actual nature.
Regarding the essence of the "entrance" (*praveśa*), which is the capacity to enter, it is, from the perspective of the non-dual ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), merely non-duality itself.

However, because one speaks of eight distinctions according to the various gates of the "object of entrance" (*praveśya*)—distinguishing between the conventional and the ultimate—the treatise below points back to the previously mentioned "object of entrance," which is precisely what is opened as eight kinds within the fundamental Mahāyāna.
Thus, with the exception of non-duality itself, there are no other gateways or dharmas apart from these.

Not taking this as the fundamental basis, yet prior to the division of the dharmas and meanings entered therein, the essence, characteristics, and functions of the mind are collectively termed the "Fundamental Mahāyāna.
Therefore, within the *Inga-fen* (Section on Causes and Conditions), these eight are specifically designated as the "General" (*zong*).
Thus, one knows that they are profound, supreme, and inconceivable. Formerly, during my years spent in Yunzhong, I personally obtained [this teaching].
A single pearl is perfectly round and increasingly pure, yet it can produce many colors within;
this serves as a metaphor for the Abhidharma (Dharmaparyāya) and illustrates the eight colors—red, purple, blue, green, and four shades of each, light and deep.

These eight colors appear distinctly and vividly all at once, yet the original pearl is fundamentally only one; depending on the color by which it is called, it is named a "deep red pearl" or a "light red pearl."
The fundamental Mahāyāna is likewise thus: its essence is originally one, yet it can manifest eight gates according to the eight modes of entry, which are termed the "Eight Mahāyānas.
In meaning, this corresponds to the *Inexhaustible Treasury Sūtra* of all Buddhas and the *Great Dhāraṇī Treasury*.
Because of this single treasury, there is nothing it does not penetrate and nothing it does not encompass; it is perfectly complete and perfectly equal, utterly equal.
All the *tathāgatagarbhas* whatsoever have none that does not take this as their root; they are like a king, like a lord, like heaven, and like the earth.
This single kind serves as the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of the support, while the various *tathāgatagarbhas* serve as the specific characteristics (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*) supported by it.
Question: Since this root is free from names and free from marks, to what destination would you lead sentient beings?

The respondent replied: "If one does not open the gate, it is indeed as you have challenged. However, if the gate is opened to accommodate the faculties so that they may enter through the gate and construct that fundamental dharma, would it not then reach [the goal]? Therefore, the subsequent treatise states:
'Because one takes a single essence and a single mind as the gate through which one enters, it is called the Mahāyāna of a single essence and a single mind,' and so forth."

Because it can produce all supramundane wholesome causes and effects, and because its functional capacity is vast as the gateway through which one enters, it is called the Mahāyāna that possesses the great functional capacity for all supramundane wholesome causes and effects.
Furthermore, regarding the previously mentioned "capacity to enter" and the eight gates, four of these gates are real and four are conventional; however, within the Dharma, [they are both].

In the two gates [of the preceding section], the order was first the ultimate (*paramārtha*) and then the conventional (*saṃvṛti*); in the six gates [of this section], the order is first the conventional and then the ultimate.
Although there is no textual explanation regarding the names and meanings of the eight gates, according to the second treatise itself, it poses the question:

"For what reason do the various treatises fully list the fundamental numbers within the established gates, yet omit those numbers when explaining them individually in the scattered gates? It answers itself: "Because one wishes to increase..."
By the power of the student’s contemplation, I now follow these instructions to provide a rough explanation as follows: First is the Gate of the Single Essence and Single Mind.

This means that, based upon the fundamental Mahāyāna, one establishes the dependent by means of the essence of principle—which is self-contained, free from dependence, pure, and wondrous—and the mind of spiritual clarity—which is self-contained and free from dependence—to guide and lead the practitioner.
Regarding the second point, the fundamental basis for entering through the gateways of the Mahāyāna in its entirety, there are two aspects:
first, the gateway of the single mind of the three natures, which likewise arises as a dependent upon the fundamental Mahāyāna;

and second, the gateway of the mind that, by means of wisdom in relation to principle, mutually contemplates their essence, characteristics, and function, and which, through this mutual contemplation and realization, guides sentient beings—this is the gateway based on the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the third [aspect], the gate of the fundamental Mahāyāna as the basis for entry, which is the essence of the immeasurable and boundless distinctions of all phenomena—
neither increasing nor decreasing— it likewise functions within the fundamental Mahāyāna to give rise to the various conventional dharmas that depend upon it,
which are mutually distinct, as well as their respective bases of mutual dependence.
The essence [of this gate] is that which receives and guides sentient beings, serving as the fundamental basis for entering through the gates; it is, in general, the Mahāyāna.
Fourth, its essence is quiescent, unmixed, of a single flavor, equal, neither increasing nor decreasing, and vast.
Furthermore, the gate also relies upon the fundamental Mahāyāna to give rise to the principle of the non-dual absolute truth (*paramārtha-satya*) which serves as the dependent, and with...
The essence that transcends all dependence serves as the basis for guiding practitioners to enter through the gates;

this fundamental basis consists of two gates—the characteristics and the functions of the Mahāyāna in general—which may be inferred from the above. Whatever dharma one enters is precisely the Middle Way, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*);
furthermore, the means of entry does not transcend the principle of the two truths, the conventional and the ultimate. Moreover, [this is] reiterated later.

Regarding the eight dharmas that constitute the entry and the basis: there is a certain class of beings who, delighting in brevity and possessing inferior faculties, hear the first "heavy gate" (*guru-dvāra*) teaching of the Dharma;

because it is profound and supreme, they are unable to understand it. The Tathāgata, through skillful guidance, further establishes the subsequent "heavy gate" teaching to transform and deliver those of such faculties.
Having heard it, they subsequently give rise to comprehension. What is the meaning of this? It means that one merely opens up the preceding fundamental [teaching].

The vehicles are divided into four types, namely: the single mind (*ekacitta*), the three greats (*trimaṇḍala*), the fundamental Mahāyāna as the basis (*āśraya*), and the single mind and the three greats as that which relies upon it (*āśrita*).

While these four, when viewed in relation to the preceding category, constitute the fundamental Mahāyāna and thus serve as the basis, when viewed in relation to the subsequent category, they are that which relies upon it. Furthermore, regarding the actual essence of what is entered, this is determined by the latter category.
Thus, although these four are the basis when contrasted with the former category—the fundamental Mahāyāna—they are now [the reliance] in relation to the latter.
The eight gates that are practiced are precisely the basis upon which four distinct types are established; they receive their names from these gates and are divided into eight kinds.

That is to say, within a single mind, two aspects are opened according to the gates: first, the "single essence Mahāyāna," wherein "single essence" refers to the gate of practice performed by the subsequent emphasis on the single mind. The dharmas entered therein receive their name from this gate. Second...
The "threefold Mahāyāna" refers to the three aspects of the subsequent "single mind" (ekacitta) as the gateway of practice; this is also designated by the name of its entryway.
Regarding its essence, characteristics, and function, it is divided into two according to the gateways, which may be understood by analogy with what precedes.

Therefore, the subsequent commentary states that the fundamental dharma of the subsequent [section] is established by its name either from the perspective of the "entry" (*praveśa*) or, as the treatise says, "alternatively" (*vā*), from the perspective of the "gate."

In essence, this principle is contained herein. Furthermore, regarding the eight gates of the subsequent "ability to enter" (*neng-ru*) and the "object of action" (*suo-zuo*), there are four gates each of the True and the Conventional.

Among these, for the two gates where the True comes first and the Conventional second, and for the six gates where the Conventional comes first and the True second, they may be understood by analogy with what precedes.

That is to say, based on the single mind, one establishes the gate of the "arising of the supported" as being identical in substance (*yi-ti*); this constitutes the "ability to enter," which accords with each [gate].
The mind is called the "gate of the single essence" (*tattva-dvāra*) and is also called the "gate of *tathatā*. Therefore, the subsequent treatise states:

"Because one takes the essence of *tathatā* as the gate through which one enters, it is designated as the 'essence. Furthermore, based on the single mind, there is the meaning of the three self-natures (*tri-svabhāva*) which act as the dependent origination;
these serve as the means of entry. Because they accord with the single mind, they are called the 'three self-nature gates,' and are also called..."

Regarding the "Gate of Arising and Ceasing," the subsequent treatise states: "Because one enters by means of the self-characteristic of the originally awakened mind (prakṛti-ādi-bodhicitta), it is designated as 'from this.
Within this mind, two gates are opened; furthermore, within its essence, two gates are also opened.
Based on the 'one-in-many' aspect of that which is entered, the gate of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is opened; based on the 'one-in-one' aspect..."
Within the "Entering" [section], the Gate of True Reality (*tattva*) is opened; within the remaining aspects and functions, two gates are each opened accordingly—this may be understood by analogy.
Question: What is the difference between these eight factors of the subsequent "Entering" section and those eight gates of the preceding "Entering" [section]?
Answer: The eight gates of the preceding section are merely the Great Totality (*mahā-dhāraṇī*), the fundamental totality of the Tathāgatagarbha.

The preceding section was able to rely on the distinct meanings of the two truths, the ultimate and the conventional; now, in this subsequent section, the fundamental reality that is entered is fully opened up as a unified whole, such that both phenomena (*dharma*) and their meaning (*artha*) constitute the Middle Way, the Truth of Ultimate Meaning (*paramārtha-satya*).

This division of phenomena and meaning into four distinct entities—namely, the essence, characteristics, and function of the mind, which become eight according to their respective gates—is presented here according to the fourfold dharmas of this treatise.

The two types of "that which is entered" (*praveśya*) within the middle [section]—namely, the Tathāgatagarbha that is distant from transformation and distant from bondage, and the Tathāgatagarbha of practice and characteristics—belong to the general totality;
how then could they be confused with the previously emphasized distinct categories of "that which enters" (*praveśaka*)?

Regarding the essence (*tattva*), characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and function (*vṛtti*), each is divided into four types, as is extensively explained in the other three treatises. It is based on this latter emphasis that [the distinctions are made].
Upon the distinct entities, there are further opened eight subsequent sections concerning the "supporting" (āśraya).

If one speaks generally regarding the "causal conditions" (hetu-pratyaya) section, they are termed the "general causal conditions" in relation to the eight fundamental dharmas in the "establishment of the thesis" (pratijñā-vyavasthāna) section.
Although the remaining twenty-four are all termed "distinct," if one regards the dharmas entered into by these subsequent sections in relation to those subsequent sections themselves...
The gate through which one enters may also be called "comprehensive" (*saṃgraha*). Why is this so?

Because it establishes two gates, because it is free from the two extremes, because it is the basis of reliance, and because it is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Therefore, the subsequent treatise states: "Mahāyāna is comprehensive.
Here, the term "comprehensive" refers to its being the comprehensive essence within these two locations—that is, it looks both upward and downward.
This is the definitive standard. As for being able to enter [the path] and being able to rely on specific meanings, there are infinite ways of subsuming these under the two truths;
however, these are merely distinct gates. Although the subsequent method and the preceding gate do not overlap, how could the two layers of "ability to enter" not be confused?
Answer: How could they not be confused? Each follows its own respective entry point, as the general and the particular differ. Why, then, should one be perplexed?

That what is broad at the beginning is abbreviated at the end further highlights their distinctiveness. As explained above, the preceding sections do not serve as the basis for the subsequent teachings;
thus, the intent of the treatise is clearly manifest, which scholars should understand.

Third, controlling and releasing the grand framework refers to the section on interpretation, which correctly elucidates the two dharmas and the two gates in the latter part, while the remainder is omitted without further explanation.

Regarding the "two dharmas": that which is entered through the gate of truth is called the "one-essence Mahāyāna dharma," and that which is entered through the gate of conventionality is called the "three-natures Mahāyāna dharma. These two kinds of dharmas correspond to the three truths.

Regarding the two gates of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*): first, opening up the meaning of absolute transcendence within the single dharma of mind is the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā-mukha*), which corresponds solely to the Truth of Reality (*satya*) among the three truths;

second, opening up the meaning of differentiation within the single dharma of mind is the gate of Arising and Ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*), which corresponds solely to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) among the three truths. To subsume the derivative into the fundamental is to realize that there is only this one mind.
The fundamental and the derivative are merely these two gates. In the gate where the fundamental and the derivative are clearly distinct, both the gate and the dharma exist;

in the gate where the fundamental and the derivative are utterly extinguished, both the gate and the dharma are quiescent. They are identical in their transcendence of language, for they are the non-dual ocean of fruition.

Furthermore, regarding the two dharmas entered by the latter [gate], they are clarified through three differences and two similarities. As for the three differences: first, the bases are different, each according to its respective prior stage.
Because the fundamental Mahāyāna serves as the basis, it is like a single father and two sons who both rely upon him;
one son represents the laity and the other the monastic community (*saṃgha*). Although they rely on the same father, each fulfills his own distinct role;

yet, from the perspective of that single father acting as their respective basis, the significance differs for each, despite the distinction between the producer and the produced. Here, we take the former [the basis].
Regarding the differences in their bases, there are two gates of difference: because the two gates of the ultimate and the conventional each have distinct modes of entry;

and regarding the third, the difference in their objects, because they each take as their object either their own respective basis, or the preceding basis, or the subsequent dependent, thus differing in their objects. As for what is said about the two being the same:
first, they are universally the same in terms of their dimensions and so forth; second, they are the same in name, because the ten names are common to both. This is repeated at the end.
One is able to enter two gates; to clarify the seven differences and one similarity, the seven differences are as follows:
first, the difference in persons, because the True Gate has the pure liberation-faculty as its root, whereas the Conventional Gate has the three groups of sentient beings as its root;
second, the difference in dharmas, because the True Gate possesses only pure dharmas, while the Conventional Gate fully possesses both defiled and pure dharmas; third, the difference in basis...
The gate of difference from reality (*tattva*) relies solely upon each individual moment of mind; the gate of the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) relies solely upon multiple moments of mind.
The practice of the fourth gate, difference from reality, consists in the non-arising of manifold thoughts; the practice of the conventional gate consists in using awakening to counteract defilement.

The essence of the fifth gate, difference from reality, is pure and equal to the fundamental [nature]; the essence of the conventional gate is characterized by defilement and distinct from the fundamental nature.

The sixth gate, "the object differs from the true," refers to the fact that it takes each individual mind as its object; the conventional gate refers to the fact that it takes many minds as its object.

The seventh gate, "the stage differs from the true," refers to the fact that the stages and grounds abide in a state of confusion; the conventional gate refers to the fact that the stages and grounds abide in a state of progression.

As for the statement "identical in one," this means they are universally identical. In the true gate, the essence is such that it is free from faults and afflictions, and its activity is non-existent.
The three provisional aspects are the perfection of the qualities of fulfillment; the three actual realities are that all phenomena are true and without delusion, such that nothing can be discarded;

all phenomena are thusness, such that no position can be established. Furthermore, based on verbal expression, the aspect of thusness-as-empty is revealed as being free from faults and afflictions, possessing no characteristics of the four propositions; the aspect of thusness-as-not-empty is the perfection of the qualities of fulfillment. Four.

The Virtue of Dharma says that there are three kinds of provisional designations (*prajñapti*): first, the provisional designation of verbal expression, because the preceding four [categories] are all unreal;

second, the provisional designation of names, because the preceding name is also unreal; third, the provisional designation of mental measurement, because the preceding nine types of mental measurement are all not real.
However, these are mostly based on the single mind which takes only the conventional gate as its object; dharmas such as *tathatā* (suchness) are spoken of according to their respective gates.
In the gate of the provisional not relying on the real, because it is the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*), it is said that there are three virtues:
first, the virtue of ultimate equality, because it is free from the basis of the four preceding false and delusive verbal expressions;

second, the virtue of being without change or variation, because it is free from the basis of the names of the nine transformations and ten variations of the non-Buddhists; third, the virtue of being indestructible, because it is free from...

Regarding the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) stated on the basis of the mental category that destroys the obstacles of afflictions through various methods and destroys the obstacles regarding the knowable:

first, the false attachment to non-existent characteristics as being truly existent, for reality is not that; second, the false attachment to non-non-existent characteristics as being truly non-existent, for reality is not that;
third, the false attachment to the "neither existent nor non-existent" characteristic as being a dual negation, for reality is not that.
For that reason, the four [alternatives] are neither characterized by existence nor characterized by non-existence; they are false attachments to both as being real.

Because they are not so, the four phrases—beginning with "not one" and so forth—are to be understood according to the previous four phrases. Since these are free from the hundred negations, all verbal expression is cut off.

As for the four virtues, they refer to the manifestation of the true mind as eternally constant and unchanging, and as fully replete with pure dharmas. First is the virtue of permanence, because it is free from...
First, because it is subject to the shifting and movement of worldly phenomena; second, because its quality of bliss is free from all suffering and oppression;
third, because its quality of self is free from the false transformations of lack of sovereignty; and fourth, because its quality of purity is free from all defiled and base dharmas.
Within this true gateway, there is only the verbal expression and mindfulness of its own gate, which constitute conformity.
Because of the discourse on True Suchness (*tathatā*), it is not said to be permanent, nor is it said to be impermanent; there is no one who can speak, and there is no dharma that is spoken.
This gateway is solely suchness (*tathatā*) and the teaching of suchness; this teaching is also called the sound of True Suchness.
Once the practitioner has heard this discourse that accords with suchness, they listen with ears that accord with suchness, and by means of this, they give rise to what accords with suchness.
Through this mental reflection, one thoroughly realizes the *tathatā* (suchness) of fulfilled virtue; yet this mental reflection is neither a thought of permanence nor a thought of impermanence.
There is no mind that can reflect, and no object upon which to reflect. This gateway consists solely of the mindfulness of quiescence and tranquility;

this mindfulness is also called the mindfulness of non-orientation. Whether it be those of faith or the virtuous, whether they be noble ones (*ārya*) or those who have attained the fruits, it applies to all accordingly.

Because they abide in a state of confusion regarding their respective stages, and because this true gateway has both the fruit of entry and the causes that lead to it, one is said to "attain entry" when, amidst this state of causal and fruitional confusion, one remains far removed from discursive speech and conceptual recollection.

Within the true gateway, all dualistic expression is absent—speech is identical to the meaning itself—and all dualistic recollection is absent—recollection is itself quiescence. Thus, the realization of the ocean of the true fruit is entirely free from these.

Therefore, within the Gate of Arising and Ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*), the ten Tathāgata-garbhas are opened forth by combining the primary and secondary [teachings]. The fourfold analysis is as follows: 1.

**Exclusively that which is entered.** The first three *garbhas* constitute the Great Treasury of Total Retention (*mahā-dhāraṇī-kośa*). This corresponds to the primary emphasis on the fundamental Mahāyāna—the distant turning away and the distant binding.

It refers to the Mahāyāna entered through the subsequent emphasis on the gate of truth (*tattva-mukha*), including its practice (*caryā*) and its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). It also includes the subsequent emphasis on the gate of conventionality (*saṃvṛti-mukha*). [End of excerpt]

Regarding the Mahāyāna entryways, there are two: first, the capacity for entry; second, the six subsequent treasuries (*pitaka*). Among these, the fourth treasury alone is the true gateway, which is the essence and characteristic of True Suchness (*tathatā*).

From the fifth treasury through the ninth treasury, all are subsumed under the nature of True Suchness within the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*), specifically the principle of the nature of True Suchness, the emptiness of the nature of deluded defilement, and the inherent virtues of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya-parāvṛtti*). Delusive phenomena are designated as "treasuries" because they are contained therein. Third.

That which is entered by means of penetration is also that which penetrates; this refers to the tenth treasury (*kośa*), or alternatively, to the single mind or the fundamental awakened mind (*mūla-bodhicitta*), because it is concealed and hidden within worldly phenomena.

Fourth, that which is neither entered nor capable of entering refers to the non-dual Mahāyāna, the ocean of ineffable fruition, because it is not a phenomenon subsumed under the aforementioned ten treasuries. Within the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*), regarding the unconditioned...
The arising and ceasing [of phenomena] open up the fourfold unconditioned: True Suchness (*tathatā*), Original Enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*), and Initial Enlightenment (*ādi-awakening*).
Space possesses two distinct bodies, yet their universal body takes as its essence the Dharma of the One Mind, which is neither existent nor non-existent.
Thus, their distinct bodies are, respectively: the principle of quiescence, the natural intrinsic wisdom, the wisdom that arises in accordance with others, and the state of non-existence.

As their essential nature, each possesses two functions. Their universal functions are, respectively: giving rise to all phenomena; not abiding in their own nature but constantly following deluded transformations;
and causing what is to exist to come into existence. Their specific functions are, respectively: being impartial; never failing in constancy; never undergoing transformation;
counteracting one's own faults; and the non-loss of emptiness. Furthermore, regarding arising and ceasing, five conditioned states are opened up.

Fundamental ignorance possesses two aspects each in its arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing; its universal essence takes the "neither existent nor non-existent" fundamental dharma of the One Mind as its substance.
Its distinct aspects take, respectively, the grossly differentiated defiled dharmas and the subtly differentiated defiled dharmas—such as the Great Power and the Dwelling Ground—as their substances.
Each thus possesses two functions: a universal function and a specific function. The universal function is non-dual.

The characteristic of arising (*jāti*) bestows power upon the characteristics of birth, abiding, change, and cessation; the characteristic of cessation bestows power upon those above it and upon itself.
Therefore, through their distinct functions, they are all able to act as obstructions wherever they reach.

Thus, the five conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) factors have power over the four unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) factors, while the five defiled factors have power, whereas the four purified factors lack power; these four are powerless.
When the four pure [aspects] operate and evolve in conjunction with the five powerful conditioned [aspects], turning their backs on the fundamental state,
this is called the "lower turning" (adhaḥ-parāvṛtti) within the indeterminate group of beings (mithyātva-niyata-rāśi) prior to the ten stages of faith, where they remain submerged without respite.

If the four unconditioned [aspects] permeate the five conditioned [aspects] such that the four pure aspects possess power while the five defiled aspects lack power, then the powerless five defilements are instead harmonized with the four pure aspects as they evolve.
Turning toward the source, from the stage of the Ten Faiths upward, practicing without ceasing is called the "superior turning.

Furthermore, within the gate of arising and ceasing, based on the meanings of existence, non-existence, the conditioned, and the unconditioned, as well as the general and specific senses, the ten *ālaya-vijñānas* are opened up through a fourfold analysis:
first, there is only the conditioned consciousness; second, from the second [ignorance] and the fifth [karma] up to the seventh [manifestation], these constitute the four treasuries.

Because all consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) are subject to flux, those consciousnesses that possess the characteristics of wisdom (*jñāna*) are either subsumed under the fundamental [consciousness] and thus included within the *ālayavijñāna*,
or they are subsumed under the derivative [consciousnesses] and are not included within the *ālayavijñāna*. The second, fourth, ninth, and fourteenth [consciousnesses],
along with the single type of *tathatā-ālaya* (the *ālaya* of suchness), constitute five types of *ālayavijñāna* that are not impermanent.

Therefore, space and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) are the "meaning" (*artha*), while [the conditioned] is the "phenomenon" (*lakṣaṇa*); since meaning follows from substance, both are subsumed within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

When the fundamental is relied upon to open up the derivative, they are not collected by the storehouse consciousness. Third, there are both conditioned consciousnesses and unconditioned consciousnesses; this refers to the Great Sovereign, the *ālayavijñāna*.
Fourth, there are neither conditioned consciousnesses nor unconditioned consciousnesses; this refers to the many aspects of the one mind, which possesses three natures.

Furthermore, in the Mahāyāna, the gate of arising and ceasing, fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*), initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*), true suchness (*tathatā*), and empty space each possess two functions, namely the specific and the universal.
Speaking from the perspective of the specific function, there are the two pure awakenings and the two pure natures;

because they are free from ignorance and do not undergo defiled perfuming, they are called "pure. Speaking from the perspective of the universal function, there are the two [types of] defiled and pure awakenings and the two [types of] defiled and pure natures.

Question: Since principle does not maintain its own nature and is well-received by defiled perfuming, it is called "defiled-purity. What are the characteristics of the two types of awakening when they successively sever defilement and realize principle?
Answer: Pure Original Awakening is neither existent nor non-existent, neither afflicted nor virtuous;

it transcends the path of names and words and is cut off from the tracks of thought and investigation. It exists solely as the suchness of reality (*dharmatā*). From this, the pure Initial Awakening arises and gives rise to wisdom.

The arousal of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the severance of delusions, and the realization of principle are designated as "original enlightenment" (*mūla-awakening*). This original enlightenment possesses three distinct functions:
first, its function of perfuming (*vāsanā*) is able to perfume the adornments of the three periods [of time] into a single awakening;

second, its function of realizing principle does not treat the two obstacles [of afflictions and cognizable objects] as separate, but constantly realizes the two principles; third, its function of acting as a condition produces numerous responsive transformations that pervade everywhere.
Because it constantly serves as the supreme condition for sentient beings whenever and wherever it is present, the pure *ārambha-awakening* (initial awakening) possesses two distinct functions:
first, the distinct function of subduing delusions; second, the distinct function of realizing principle. It gives rise to great power of wisdom and great power of meditative concentration;
it thoroughly subdues both obstructions by understanding that their fundamental nature is empty, and it constantly realizes both principles. This is...

Whether coarse or subtle, whether fundamental or derivative, these five types of conditioned phenomena are universally illumined by the principle of non-existence; this is called the severance of defilement.
The original enlightenment of purity possesses four universal functions: first, the universal function of treating delusions; second, the universal function of realizing the principle.
From fundamental ignorance up to the cessation of characteristics, ultimate wisdom is awakened to illumine that the principle of delusion is also non-existent.

1. Realizing the two principles, it is appropriate that they correspond to defilement and purity; thus, from the subtle to the coarse, from the root to the branches, these five types of conditioned phenomena are illuminated according to their principles, and this is called the third [aspect], "severance," because there is no further teaching. 2. The universal application of the manifested realm:

it can manifest the six Buddhas and give rise to the six realms, responding to and transforming beings for their benefit and happiness, as its timing and location are all-pervasive. 3. The universal application of the secondary afflictions.

Because it does not maintain its own nature but follows conditions to become delusion, this awakening is said to turn its back on the holy and face toward the ordinary, entering the ground of error and the ocean of the storehouse of ignorance where movement never ceases; thus, the defiled and pure initial awakening possesses four universal functions:
first, the universal function of following afflictions, wherein within the group of those fixed in error, one constantly follows defilement even before encountering the instruction of a teacher.
Because they function in constant conjunction, (1) they are universally applicable for subduing delusions;
because they are universally applicable for realizing principle, (2) when one encounters the teacher’s instruction from the stage of the ten faiths onward, they initiate pure functioning.

From the cessation of lower characteristics up to great ignorance, through the wisdom of partial and complete fulfillment, they sever false defilements and progressively realize those two principles of defilement and purity; therefore, this is taught.

First, awakening consists of turning one’s back on the mundane and facing toward the sacred, reaching the stage of Vajra, which is termed the Path of Liberation and named the State of Wondrous Awakening.

Second, returning to the source through universal application, wherein one enters the fruit-stage without distinguishing between the beginning and the foundation. Third, the four types of awakening are perfectly integrated as a single awakening;

the four principles are without discrepancy as they constitute a single principle. Fourth, wisdom and its object are non-dual, in perfect accord with the source of the mind, though this state is ultimately beyond conceptualization.

All marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are also without cessation; they are wondrously wondrous, profoundly profound, tranquil, and limpid, immediately submerging into the perfect, ultimate, and sovereign non-dual Mahāyāna fruit-ocean that transcends words. Therefore, regarding the severance of delusions, there should be four propositions:
first, sudden rather than gradual, which refers to pure *ādi-bodhi* (initial awakening); second, gradual rather than sudden, which refers to defiled and pure *ādi-bodhi*.
The third awakening is both sudden and gradual: this refers to the fundamental awakening of defilement and purity, which is termed "sudden" in terms of time and "gradual" in terms of its stages.

The fourth is neither sudden nor gradual: this refers to the fundamentally pure fundamental awakening, which, regarding the delusions of both the root and the branches, has no gradual or sudden severance.

As for the relationship between the fundamentally pure fundamental awakening and the fundamental awakenings of defilement and purity—if one examines them by way of their identity or difference, they are identical in terms of essence.
It is said that they are not identical because their meanings differ, yet they are not distinct because they are both identical and different, and neither identical nor different.
As it is with the two kinds of original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*), so too should the meaning of the two kinds of initial enlightenment (*ādi-awakening*) be understood accordingly.
The distinction between identity and difference regarding the two pure enlightenments arises because there is pure initial enlightenment based upon pure original enlightenment.

Awakening, moreover, begins from purity; thus, the "awakening that realizes" (prativedha-bodhi) is established as the "fundamental awakening of purity" (viśuddha-mūla-bodhi). Whether considered from the perspective of their distinct meanings, they are different names for the same essence;

or whether considered from the perspective of their identical substance, they are the same essence without being different types. Therefore, one should follow this principle: they are both the same and different, neither identical nor distinct.
Just as it is with the two types of pure awakening, so too should it be understood regarding the two types of defiled and pure awakening.

Furthermore, within the gate of arising and ceasing, there are two gates: the gate of the four characteristics and the gate of subsequent awakening. Regarding the first gate, the four characteristics have four aspects:

(1) the coarse and heavy affliction of the four characteristics, which refers to the four characteristics over a long period, meaning they are only fully exhausted and abandoned upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood from the stage of faith onwards;
(2) the subtle affliction of the four characteristics, which refers to the four characteristics over a short period.

Because phenomena existing through mutual conditions possess the moments [of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing], once the coarse and heavy [defilements] have been severed, the subtle [defilements] no longer exist; thus, there are three merits of impermanence.

Fourth, because the characteristics of the faults are the reverse of the characteristics of the merits, the name "merit" is established. As soon as the characteristics of the faults arise, the characteristics of the merits arise accordingly.
The virtues of the merits and the darkness of the faults are equal, and this serves as a fitting analogy. It is called "just beginning to arise" for this reason.

Regarding the four marks of impermanence and the four marks of the eternally abiding merits: while the latter two kinds of merit have their marks arising only now, these merits were originally present.

Therefore, from the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) up to the ten stages of the bodhisattva (*bhūmi*), because the realization of the causal stage still involves the subtle afflictions (*kleśa*) of subsequent stages, they remain permeated by them; thus, one cannot fully comprehend the faults [of the causal stage]. (4)
Because the characteristics are identical with merit, as in the stage of the ten faiths, one realizes that the characteristic of cessation is actually a fault;

by ceasing it so that it does not arise again, this is called "perfuming-separation" (*vāsanā-viyoga*). However, because one has not yet understood that the original nature of the characteristic of cessation is inherently pure and is actually merit, this is called "perfuming-togetherness" (*vāsanā-sahabhū*).
Furthermore, this perfuming-togetherness flows on until the tenth stage, where one merely understands the four characteristics.
The faults to be abandoned are the four marks of the unawakened; the pure virtues to be realized extend up to the ultimate *samyak-saṃbodhi* at the stage of Buddhahood.
Where the four marks of faults are exhausted, there the merits of the four marks are perfected.
When only faults exist, one establishes merits; yet once faults are departed from, merits also vanish. Because there is impermanence, [there is suffering].
Once the notions of permanence and impermanence have been established and both permanence and impermanence have been discarded, what remains?

Since the four characteristics—the objects of treatment and the objects of knowledge—are not established, where can the various awakenings that treat them and know them reside? In reality, there are no distinctions between the fifty-one stages of initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*);

by uniting initial awakening with the fundamental, they are but a single, wondrous awakening that perfectly accords with the source of the mind. It merges into the ocean of fruition and subsequently follows along.
Regarding the gate of awakening that accords with defilement, there is the initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) from the stage of the ten faiths onward, which is distinguished by two gates:

First is *pūrṇa-bodhi* (complete awakening), which refers to the ultimate initial awakening at the stage of Buddhahood. In contrast to the preceding partial awakenings, this is termed complete awakening.

When comparing the partial to the complete, all preceding partial awakenings are also called non-awakening (*abodhi*). These various stages of complete awakening continue until the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), at which point they cease to exist.

Second, the two are combined into one awakening because they are identical to original awakening (*mūla-awakening*) and without distinction. Second, they are divided awakenings because they fully manifest both awakening and non-awakening.
For instance, at the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), one has already departed from the mark of cessation and no longer receives the perfuming of that mark of cessation;
therefore, it is called "awakening. Yet, this very initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) receives the perfuming of the defilements of subsequent stages.

It is still termed "non-awakening" (abodha), just as gold ore, because it is free from coarse impurities, may be called "gold," yet as long as it is not free from subtle impurities, it is also called "gold ore.
However, the gold that is free from coarse impurities and the gold that remains with subtle impurities do not differ in their essential nature; how could there be any distinction?

It is like the difference between awakening that is free from the characteristic of cessation and awakening that retains the characteristics of arising and so forth—their essence of awakening is the same.

Since their essence is without distinction, how could they be different? Therefore, the *Śāstra* states: "Awakening and non-awakening are mutually inclusive and interpenetrating; they are of one single flavor. Is this not what that refers to? Just as it is with the ten stages of faith, so it is with the noble ones and sages (*ārya*). The fourth stage is the fulfillment of the causes; the fifth stage is the fulfillment of the fruits. Based on the four characteristics of that which is to be remedied (*vipakṣa*), the five stages of the remedy (*pratipakṣa*) are established.
Within the stage of arising, distinctions are made between the coarse and the subtle, thereby establishing the two stages of the fulfillment of causes and the fulfillment of fruits.
In the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), four factors are fully present: first, the person who practices; second, the cause that is practiced; third, one’s own stage; [and fourth, the fruit].

Regarding the four types of perfuming and the separation from the three characteristics in the stage of fruition: the three stages of worthiness (*tri-kalyāṇa*) and the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*) all possess these four. Only in the stage of the fulfillment of fruition do there remain three matters:
first, the person who is fully perfected; second, the counteractive practice; and third, the characteristic of ultimate fulfillment.

In the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), one is separated from the characteristic of extinction (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*). In the three stages of worthiness, one abandons the characteristic of difference (*bhinna-lakṣaṇa*). In the nine stages, one abandons the characteristic of abiding (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*). There are four aspects to this characteristic of abiding.

On the first stage (*bhūmi*), one eliminates the characteristic of continuity (*saṃtati-lakṣaṇa*) until it is exhausted; from the second stage through the seventh, one eliminates the characteristic of cognition (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*);

on the eighth stage, one eliminates the manifest characteristic (*pratibhāsa-lakṣaṇa*); on the ninth stage, one eliminates the characteristic of transformation (*pariṇāma-lakṣaṇa*); and on the tenth stage, one eliminates the characteristic of birth (*janman-lakṣaṇa*).

Within this elimination of the characteristic of birth, the coarse portion of the "conjoined movement" (*sahaja-saṃyukta-spanda*) is eliminated during the stage where the fruit is fulfilled, while the subtle portion remains.

The fundamental ignorance of the differentiated aspect of the karma of individuality then vanishes into the perfect initial enlightenment (*samyak-prativedha*), merging with the original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) and reaching the ocean of fruition.

Thus, within the original enlightenment of defilement and purity, there are two types of dependent aspects: the aspect of the reliance on the function of severing defilement, which constitutes the aspect of pure wisdom (*jñāna-viśuddhi-lakṣaṇa*);
and the aspect of the reliance on the function of manifesting objects, which constitutes the aspect of inconceivable karma (*acintya-karma-lakṣaṇa*). Within the aspect of pure wisdom...

Furthermore, it possesses two powers capable of counteracting two obstructions: (1) the power of the Dharma and the power of fulfillment, which sever fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*) and the karma-phase of the solitary aspect;
according to principle, these further counteract one portion of the subtle delusions of the combined and moving aspects to manifest the *dharmakāya*.
(2) The power of reality and the power of fulfillment, which sever the combined and moving aspects as well as the evolving and appearing aspects.
It is pure because the wisdom of distinct characteristics and the wisdom of the characteristic of continuity are thoroughly purified;
furthermore, within the characteristic of inconceivable karma, it can manifest the six objects such as form, and can manifest the six responsive and transformational Buddhas.

It pervades the three periods of time without moving, encompasses the ten directions in a single thought-moment without dividing, and benefits sentient beings according to their faculties without interruption. Therefore, it is pure.

Fundamental awakening has four functional applications; because their meanings are identical to those of a mirror, it is also called the "four mirrors. First is the Mirror of Reality-as-Such Emptiness (*tathatā-śūnyatā*).
The mind that is free from discursive thought is called "as-it-is" (*tathatā*); being free from false objects, it is called "reality" (*tathatā*).

The single character "emptiness" (*śūnya*) carries the meaning of being utterly remote [from delusion]. Just as the wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*) pervades all things yet does not manifest other reflections, it is solely identical [to its own nature].

The analogy of the pearl manifesting reflections clearly illustrates how the principles may be understood through correspondence: the two causes—the permeation of the mirror and the permeation of the three worlds—result in the single fruit of awakening.

Just as when a bright, shining pearl is placed amidst myriad things, the pearl permeates all things so that they all become luminous and pure, and thus the pearl and the objects mutually manifest one another;
the principle may be examined in detail in this way. Far removed from the four faults, the three dharmas abide eternally within the one mind.

The mirror of renunciation: it renounces three faults and perfects three virtues. It is like a pearl that, when separated from [corruptive substances], effectively removes turbid dust and remains only as pure water;
yet if placed in a stinking forest, it can produce fine fragrance while obstructing foul odors. The mirror of the four conditions of perfuming (*vāsanā*) means:
taking birth as a condition and the drawing forth by a Buddha as a condition, they perfume one to cultivate goodness and cause mindfulness to manifest accordingly. Thus is the analogy.

Just as a single pearl reflects the colors of many surrounding pearls because it manifests various reflections according to them, so too, within the context of non-awakening, the six types of ignorance are distinguished.
First, regarding the discourse on ignorance within awakening: when one grasps the sun of perfect *prajñā*, there is immediate purification.

Second, regarding the fundamental awakening that accompanies defilement: through the remedy for delusion, one realizes the principle; this involves the universal illumination of the functional application and the fundamental awakening that accompanies defilement.

Because the ultimate perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-abhisambodhi*) following the path of liberation through initial awakening (*ādi-bodha*) leaves not a single dharma unilluminated, the five meanings of "non-explanation" (*avyākaraṇa*) and the five meanings of "explanation" (*vyākaraṇa*) are established.
These [five meanings] refer exclusively to the full knowledge that can know; the two types of darkness—ignorance (*avidyā*) and non-illumination—are separately opened into ten kinds.
Though their names differ, their essence is the same, being subsumed solely within fundamental non-awakening (*mūla-avidyā*). This refers exclusively to...
The eye can cause delusion, and when these three [eye, object, and consciousness] arise together, they are all ignorance (*avidyā*).

Because they universally grasp all phenomena within the single gateway of arising and ceasing, which possess two characteristics, they can act as the material basis for illusions among illusory people, and act as the material basis for virtues among virtuous people.
This is just as two eyes see differently in the darkness of night; ordinary beings and Buddhas observe the phenomena of illusion and virtue with distinct perspectives.
Therefore, this is based solely on the objects that are deluded about and cognized, which are designated as fundamental ignorance;

for within that mirror, there are fully present the physical, mental, and intellectual wisdoms. Thus, the four categories—neither-existence-nor-non-existence, neither-arising-nor-ceasing, neither-affirmation-nor-negation, and neither-dependence-nor-independence—are fundamentally non-existent. However, all phenomena are by nature originally empty and cannot be made clear.

5. Because phenomena ultimately result in ineffability and depend upon the cessation of mental activity, the ignorance of emptiness clearly realizes that both the essence and function of the purely imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) are empty, just as the essence and function of a rabbit’s horn are clearly understood to be non-existent.
6. Within the gate of birth through the perfection of ignorance, the Great Gathering Lord Consciousness possesses awakening and does not [perceive] it.

Awakening is able to encompass and give rise to all defiled and pure states; thus, these six kinds of fundamental ignorance are designated according to their meanings to illustrate the mutual manifestation of the true and the false, and to distinguish between mind and object.
When their essential nature is precisely identified, they are nothing other than the Great Encompassing Sovereign Consciousness, and therefore there is no difference.
With ignorance as the cause, it can give rise to the three subtle states: first, the *karmic mark* (*karmalakṣaṇa*), wherein subject and object are undifferentiated.
First, the "perfuming aspect" (mūn-ch'eng wang-so) refers to the movement of the awakening mind caused solely by the perfuming of ignorance; this is termed "karma.
Second, the "evolving aspect" (chuan-hsiang) refers to the arising of views based on that movement, which is capable only of what has not yet been accomplished; this is termed "evolution.
Third, the "manifesting aspect" (hsien-hsiang) refers to the transformation of objects based on those views, wherein both subject and object are fully present; this is termed the "manifested object."

Taking the *dhātus* as conditions, there arises the first of the six coarse [aspects], the subtle differentiation of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) accompanied by the clinging to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).

This gives rise to feelings of aversion or attachment toward favorable or unfavorable objects; this is the second, the "aspect of continuity" (*anubandha-lakṣaṇa*), which is also a subtle differentiation of the mental consciousness’s clinging to phenomena.

Based on the preceding aspect of cognition, it produces feelings of suffering or pleasure, giving rise to powerful volitions and continuous thoughts that do not cease; this is the third, "clinging" (*grāha*).

Fourth, the characteristic of grasping at signs of names is also coarse; it arises from the consciousness associated with the human-grasping (*pudgala-grāha*) that follows the previous [grasping], which takes up objects through continuous recollection and gives rise to attachment.

Fifth, the characteristic of performing actions consists of meritorious actions, non-meritorious actions, and immovable actions, which arise from the consciousness associated with the human-grasping that follows the previous false conceptualization, engaging in successive conceptualizations of conventional designations (*prajñapti*).

Because the general and specific causes of movement and activity constitute the essence of karma; because the general and specific categories of retribution in the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm constitute the essence of the fruit of the six feelings;
and based on these general principles, the characteristics of similarity and difference are revealed:
all pure dharmas are subsumed under awakening-mind (*bodhicitta*), while all defiled dharmas are subsumed under non-awakening. This collectively encompasses all defilements.

The gates of the identical nature (*samāna-lakṣaṇa*) and the different nature (*visama-lakṣaṇa*), which clarify the true intent of composing this treatise by examining the similarities and differences between pure awakening and non-awakening, are as follows:
Within the gate of identical nature, all defiled and pure states of awakening and non-awakening are nothing other than the single True Suchness (*tathatā*); there is no separate dharma whatsoever.
They are like the fine dust of a clay vessel or the moist nature of various waves—they are simply True Suchness. Within the gate of different nature...
It reveals that the single True Suchness manifests as all phenomena, possessing distinct names for the defiled and the pure, and differing aspects for awakening and delusion;

yet, while these divisions are individually differentiated and possess distinct functions, they are entirely non-dual. This is the Gate of Arising and Ceasing. Furthermore, based on the defiled dharmas, it clarifies three pairs of sixfold causes and conditions.
Regarding the first two pairs of causes and conditions: the first is the cause and condition of non-correspondence, which is Original Awakening (*mūla-awakening*).

Ignorance (*avidyā*) serves as the causal condition for the essence of fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) and the three consciousnesses; fundamental awakening serves as the cause and the three characteristics serve as the conditions.
Ignorance serves as the cause for the three characteristics and the three consciousnesses serve as the conditions. Regarding the two types of corresponding causes and conditions:

the manifesting consciousness (*ādarśa-vijñāna*) takes the manifestation of forms as its causal condition; the manifesting consciousness serves as the cause for the phenomenal consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*) and coarse characteristics serve as the conditions for the manifestation of forms.

It acts as the cause for the coarse characteristics (*sthūla-lakṣaṇa*) and as the condition for the phenomenal consciousness (*vastu-vijñāna*). Regarding the next two layers of cause and condition: first, the universal pervasive cause;
because fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*), which follows along with defilement, acts as the cause and condition for that sixfold coarseness (*ṣaṭ-sthūla*).

Alternatively, it refers to the mutual functioning of cause and condition between [ignorance and] the consciousnesses; or it refers simply to acting as the cause and condition for them in their general aspect, encompassing all without distinguishing between direct and indirect.
Regarding the "bestowing of power" (*sahakāri-pratyaya*), there are two ways of explaining how the karma performed and the fruit received act as causal conditions for one another;

the following sections should be understood by analogy with these two. At the end, concerning the pervasive causal condition (*sarvatraga-hetu*): the fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) is the primary state, while ignorance (*avidyā*) is its derivative;
since this derivative karma corresponds to the three marks [of existence], it necessarily possesses causal conditions. Therefore, [it is not the case that there are no causes].
Since the manifestation of the characteristics has already been explained previously, the latter two types of causal conditions are as follows:

first, the downward-and-upward causal condition, which begins with ignorance and ends with karmic retribution; it proceeds through successive stages from the lowest to the highest, providing mutual support without interruption to function as a causal condition.
Second, the upward-and-downward causal condition, which begins with karmic retribution and ends with ignorance; it proceeds from the lowest to the highest in successive stages.

Furthermore, because each successive segment [of the continuum] bestows power upon the next without interruption by acting as a causal condition, it is further stated that the manas undergoes eleven or twelve transformations.

Regarding the eleven aspects of the mind: one is fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*), while the remaining ten consist of the three—karma, transformation, and manifestation—along with the continuity of gnosis (*jñāna*).

Since these are each explained according to their respective characteristics of consciousness (*vijñāna-lakṣaṇa*), they constitute ten types; when the fundamental [ignorance] is added, [there are eleven].

When awakening is realized, it constitutes the twelve questions. Regarding the distinction between the ten intermediate mental states (*manas*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), the answer further adds that their retinues and defiled phenomena each possess two meanings:

first, the meaning of spiritual discernment, which begins from the momentum of original awakening (*mūla-awakening*) and is established as "consciousness" because it is a state of cognitive penetration that accords with original awakening; second, the meaning of darkness and dullness, which begins from... [text fragment ends].
The momentum of ignorance gives rise to and establishes what is termed "characteristic" (*nimitta*); this characteristic turns away from the fundamental and accords with ignorance.
Because ignorance is the root of fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*), it does not separately distinguish the differences between characteristics and consciousness. There are two meanings to this:
first, the sense of "root," because it is capable of producing; second, the sense of "body," because it serves as the basis for consciousness in relation to its source.
Awakening (*bodhi*) is the cause because it is proximate; ignorance (*avidyā*) is the condition because it is remote.

With respect to their characteristics, ignorance is the cause and original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) is the condition, for both the characteristic-aspect (*nimitta*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) possess the sense of being the basis for arising;

thus they are established as being named "mind" (*manas*). Among the six coarse aspects, the latter four are in fact all "mind," though they are mentioned here only briefly. Furthermore, [this] continues...

Consciousness possesses two functional meanings: first, regarding its own substance as a continuum—explained in terms of the adherence to phenomena—the term "continuum" is established as a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound), meaning "the consciousness that is the continuum.
Second, it causes the continuum of others to maintain the cycle of birth and death without interruption; here, the term "continuum-consciousness" is established as a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound).
Furthermore, according to this latter functional meaning, there are three aspects: first, this consciousness is able to give rise to and moisten the afflictions of karma.

First, it maintains the power and efficacy of the wholesome and unwholesome karma arising from ignorance throughout immeasurable past kalpas, ensuring that these result in actualized fruits without loss.

Second, this consciousness further gives rise to the afflictions that moisten rebirth, enabling already established karma to summon the retribution of present and future suffering and pleasure without error. Third, this consciousness...

Furthermore, it is able to take as its object a progressively broader range of conceptualization with even stronger force; it gives rise to minds of pleasure or displeasure toward objects previously experienced, and gives rise to attachment or aversion toward objects present before one.
Taking as its object objects not yet known, it remains in a state of obscure non-comprehension, whereby false imaginings increase further and further, giving rise to longing.
Thus, its capacity for continuity belongs solely to the subtle mind (*manas*), and the phenomena to which this continuity applies are universal.
