regarding the subsequent explanation according to the text, there are three parts. First, answering the preceding question, which has two sub-sections; first, the number of dharmas that are perfumed.
"Infusing a single dharma-realm (up to: because it is not the support of another.
The commentary explains that the subsequent detailed exposition of the characteristics of infusion has two parts. First, the infusion of a single dharma-realm: first a question, then an answer;
within the answer, there is further a verse response. The treatise’s explanation cites a sūtra as proof, stating that within the single dharma of mind, there are two types of mastery.
Ignorance merely perfumes the sovereign dharma of the single mind, which is conditioned;

yet this dharma is fundamentally not conditioned, but receives its name only from that which perfumes it. Because this is the sovereignty of the conditioned, the designation of the sovereignty of the unconditioned is likewise established.
Regarding the phrase "perfuming the True Suchness (up to) because it is not for subsequent use":

the commentary explains that the subsequent perfuming of the four unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) involves ignorance perfuming only True Suchness in its universal application, while the remaining three unconditioned phenomena are also perfumed by it in their universal application.
Regarding the measure of the time of perfuming: because it does not involve a separate grasping [of the object].

The commentary states: This next response answers the subsequent question concerning the precise duration of perfuming; it is not a simultaneous grasping of the beginning, middle, and end as a single moment.
Rather, it may be based on the "beginning and end" within a single thought-moment (*kṣaṇa*), or it may refer to the "initial and final limits" of a single lifetime, explained in terms of delusion.
Because they exist simultaneously.

Regarding what is here called "that which is perfumed" (*bhāvya*), the commentary explains that there are three parts to the subsequent interpretation of the meaning of perfuming (*vāsanā*). First, it raises the question and explains the meaning of the perfumer (*bhāvaka*) and the perfumed (*bhāvya*), as well as their characteristics.

How is it that the perfuming agents (vāsana) are ninefold? Because they draw forth their corresponding objects of perfuming (vāsyamāna), coalesce with them as a single entity, and proceed in simultaneous conjunction;
and because the objects of perfuming lack independent power and always accord with and do not oppose the perfuming agents.

What is called "perfuming" (vāsana) has the meaning of striking and activating, just as when water and milk are poured together, they blend and harmonize, mutually [interpenetrating] without separation.
This is because the reverse is not the case; they do not mutually perfuse to form seeds through the characteristics of dharmas.
That is to say, the five conditioned dharmas (up to) function simultaneously in a common purpose.
The commentary states: Next, by pointing to these dharmas, it is shown that the five kinds of conditioned phenomena universally permeate the four unconditioned phenomena and the one [unconditioned].
Because the five dharmas perfumed by the dharma-realm and the five perfuming agents do not oppose or contradict one another, but proceed and evolve together,
they fulfill the meaning of perfuming.
Therefore, it is said that "arising and ceasing are in harmonious union."
The commentary concludes by returning to the root treatise:
"As with great ignorance... [it] should be understood in this way.
The commentary subsequently provides an analogy for other perfumings: just as great ignorance can perfume the single mind, so too do the conditioned factors exercise sovereignty over it.

Furthermore, since the meaning of the perfuming that triggers the four kinds of unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) penetrative functions is thus, the same applies to the other four conditioned (saṃskṛta) [factors] perfuming the five [consciousnesses].
Such meanings as these are clearly established by their underlying principles.

The commentary on the latter section of the sub-commentary has two parts: first, the distinction between general and specific functions—whereby they differ in receiving perfuming yet are identical in being permeated;
second, the difference between the two types of mastery and the two types of activity when compared to one another, which is termed "non-one. Within each mental dharma, the conditioned self-nature...

The fact that the four unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta) are non-different from the five conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta) in their principle of being conjoined with the perfuming agent (*vāsaka*) and the function of thorough penetration (*pariccheda-kriyā*) is termed "non-different" (*ananya*). This is because it is not taught here that the five kinds of conditioned phenomena and the two kinds of functions differ in principle;
thus, they are termed "non-one" (*aneka*). Furthermore, it is also not taught that the five kinds of conditioned phenomena possess only the function of thorough penetration.
Because there is no principle by which the activity of the perfuming agent (*kṣobhaka*) and the dharma that is perfumed (*bhāvya*) are distinct, it is said to be "not different" (*ananya*);
one must examine this minutely to understand it thoroughly.
Furthermore, from "the perfumed... up to "...is called not different."

The commentary states: Later, the distinction between the object of perfuming and the perfumer, their identity within a single mind, the fact that they are both perfumed, the fact that the unconditioned is the perfumer while the conditioned is the perfumed, and the difference between the defiled and the pure—these are why they are called "not one.
Furthermore, because the defiler and the purified are not separate from the single mind in the ultimate sense (paramārtha-satya), they are called "not different."
It is called the "Perfected Syllable" (*pūrṇākṣara*).

The commentary states: the four or five syllables that form the name of the *ālayavijñāna*—namely, the first one among the ten *li-ya* (Sanskrit: *laya*) syllables, taken either specifically as the first or inclusively as all ten—are thus termed "perfected."
Having explained the downward-turning gate (*adhaḥ-pravṛtti-mukha*), the upward-turning gate (*ūrdhva-pravṛtti-mukha*) is now explained.

first is the introductory summary: "If one wishes to establish [the point] that others come to rely upon me..."
The commentary states: Next, the cited scriptural passage contains two turns.
This scriptural passage [up to this point] constitutes the first turn.
The commentary further explains that the subsequent interrogation and exposition has two parts; first is the general question and answer.
What is the meaning of this? It refers to the downward-turning gate (*adhaḥpravṛtti-mukha*).
The commentary explains that there are four subsequent distinct sections: first, the general inquiry regarding the initial phrase of the downward turning;

second, the brief explanation below, which clarifies how fundamental awakening (*mūla-awakening*) is permeated by ignorance (*avidyā*) to form the downward-turning gate; the text is explicit and thus easily understood.
If one wishes to establish [the argument] up to this point, these words must be retained.
The commentary states: "Second, clarifying the upward transition, the treatise's sentences are re-established and the Buddha’s sūtras are reorganized;
by reversing the downward transition, they are made into an upward permeation. To accord with its own text while supporting the evidence of others—how could anyone not admire such ultimate subtlety?"
From "Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa" to "omitting faults and errors," the commentary explains the intent of the three expositions of the treatise.

The commentary states: Regarding the locus of the four fingers, having already explained the gate of upward progression, next is explained the gate of comprehensive establishment.
The commentary states: There are two types of the three gates of establishment; first, the summary of the fingers.
Regarding the "differentiation of the various consciousnesses" (up to) "how many kinds of consciousness":
the commentary explains that there are two parts to this initial exposition. First, it asks: how many are the various consciousnesses, and which sūtra speaks of how many kinds?
The verse says: "...because it is clearly explained. The commentary states:

The latter answer has two parts. First, the summary verse generally relies upon the holy teachings of the entire dispensation to explain the increase in the number of consciousnesses, ranging from a single kind up to ten.
As for the phrase "returning to the source" and so forth, this refers collectively to the "one mind" and so on.
These ten consciousnesses are enumerated and explained in such sūtras as the *Ekacitta-ālaya*; they are not taught in the *Pratyāgama-sūtra*.
Therefore, the claim that they "return to the root" is merely the number one hundred within the category of "one hundred roots," and must be an error in transcription.

The *Commentary* explains: the subsequent explanation of the text has three parts. First, a general reference and a general inquiry; it refers to the ten kinds and inquires about the ten characteristics.
"First" (up to) "What are the four? The commentary states:
Next, there are eleven distinct establishments and distinct explanations. Regarding the first consciousness, there are three parts:
first, the heading and inquiry; [the first] (up to) "...is not established."
The commentary states: Next, there are four distinct explanations. First, based on the single mind, many [minds] arise;

the single consciousness of the mind possesses all capacities, and because it is sovereign and possesses various powers such that there is nothing it cannot do, one consciousness is established rather than others.
The second [point], up to "because it is the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).

The commentary states: Based on the two *ālaya* sūtras, this should be understood as encompassing the primary *ālayavijñāna*. That which possesses the sense of obstruction consists of the five conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) dharmas;

that which possesses the sense of non-obstruction consists of the four unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas. These nine dharmas collectively serve as the basis, which constitutes the "Great Encompassment" (*mahā-saṃgraha*).
Master. Thirdly, [it is so called] because there is nothing it does not do. The commentary states:
According to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā*, this manas-consciousness possesses eleven types, namely, great ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth.
Because the five aspects and the five consciousnesses perform all functions;
fourth, because [it performs] seven matters without remainder.
The commentary states: "The four reliances and the seven transformative scriptures show that this single mental consciousness possesses seven transformations, just like a magician."
Just as it is transformed into seven people while the foolish perceive them as seven consciousnesses, yet there is only a single mental consciousness— the meaning of the illusionist is likewise so.
This is called the establishment [of the doctrine] up to the four kinds of sūtras.
The commentary states: The subsequent conclusion is based on two [points], because it provides an extensive explanation. The commentary further states:

The two pairs of consciousnesses—the ālayavijñāna as the basis for citation, termed the "discerning consciousness" (*vijñaptivijñāna*)—and the active, manifest *manovijñāna* possess functional activity.

The commentary states: Regarding the subsequent section on "Purifying Initial Awakening," there are three parts. First, the connection between the preceding and the following:
Why is this so? [It continues] until the request is made as follows. The commentary further states:
Next, based on the text, the analysis of the characteristics has two parts. First, the inquiry consists of four sections: (1) citing and pointing to [the subject] for the purpose of...
In establishing the pure *ādi-bodhi* (initial awakening), he first extends an inquiry.
As for the nature of the question: "What is meant by 'original awakening' (*mūla-bodhi*)?

The commentary explains that there are two ways of interpreting this question. First, it addresses the objection: "The *dharmakāya* inherently possesses the qualities of its nature (*dharmatā-guṇa*). This is the explanation.
The primary meaning [of "fundamental"] is that which is eternally constant, luminous and pure, and eternally constant, sovereign, which is precisely the meaning of awakening.

If one designates this as "fundamental awakening" (mūla-awakening) based on this meaning, I wish to inquire: at what time and by what means does this awakening come to possess its inherent qualities and virtues such that it is established as being named "fundamental awakening"?
If one were to speak thus (up to) its establishment, the commentary explains that there are three points of inquiry and three explanations.
First, the inquiry into whether it is not the original awakening (*mūla-avabodha*). First, the opponent's defense is cited; second, that defense is refuted.
If it is said that this awakening possesses the perfect virtue of wisdom that eliminates afflictions, then this original awakening has not yet eliminated them.
If, when delusion exists, the enlightened qualities (guṇa) are hidden, and only upon their total cessation are the enlightened qualities revealed,

how could this accord with the principle that they are primordially and eternally luminous and pure? Furthermore, since delusion precedes awakening and concealment precedes manifestation, how could this conform to the principle that [the nature] is naturally and eternally present as the fundamental basis?
"If one were to say [this], up to the point that it is not that original enlightenment (mūla-awakening)," the commentary explains:
Next, the text interrogates this initial awakening (ādi-bodhi). It first restates the opponent's defense and then refutes that defense.

If [the qualities] are eternally severed, they are simply the severance of the original; if they are eternally possessed, they are simply the possession of the original. This would then be merely initial awakening; what connection would it have with original enlightenment?
Therefore, the meaning of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-awakening*) is also not established. Why is this?

It is because original enlightenment lacks the merit of subsequent awakening (*abhisambodhi*), and thus lacks the fault of non-awakening; yet, it is precisely by being free from these two that it is called "original enlightenment.
As the subsequent treatise states: "Pure original enlightenment is neither fault nor merit. Here, however, we speak of its virtues.

If afflictions are originally accomplished, then one need not further accomplish awakening; if they are originally possessed, then one need not further possess them; and if they are originally severed, then one need not further sever them.
Since this is solely initial awakening (ādikṣānti-bodhi), what concern does it have with original awakening (mūla-bodhi)?
"Therefore" (up to) "is called original enlightenment.
The commentary explains that this subsequently cites scriptural authority to establish the proof.
For what reason (up to) "why is this so"? It asks for the underlying meaning.

The commentary states: Regarding the four questions concerning the causes, why is it that among the intrinsic qualities of the *dharmakāya*, one takes refuge and relies upon it, designating it as "original enlightenment" (*mūlapratyavekṣaṇajñāna*)?
The meaning of "original enlightenment" [extends] to directly resolving those doubts.
The commentary states that there are two parts to the subsequent resolution of doubts. First, the general response, which also has two parts. First, the citation and reference:
from "Master Aśvaghoṣa" up to "the sphere of mental activity ceases.
The commentary then provides a detailed explanation, which also has two parts. First, regarding the cessation of words and thoughts, the Master generally states: "The fundamental nature is pure."
It is devoid of all arising and ceasing; it does not exist by being established as having existence, nor is it non-existent by being slandered as having non-existence.
Thus, both faults and virtues are quiescent in their mutual dependence, and the designations of names and words, as well as the objects of mental conceptualization, are entirely cut off.
"Yet there are verbal designations (up to) the term 'original enlightenment' (*mūla-awakening*, *prakṛti-awakening*).

The commentary states: "The original nature is subsequently revealed through the initial cause; it is called 'original enlightenment' because its perfect qualities of nature are manifested when the pure initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) gives rise to wisdom and meditative concentration, reaching its ultimate limit in time and space, and because these qualities that remedy faults are established as 'pure original enlightenment' in contrast to the pure initial awakening."
Regarding the meaning of "original enlightenment" (*mūla-awakening*), the Root Treatise states that it is spoken in contrast to "initial enlightenment" (*ādi-awakening*).
This is because initial enlightenment [is established] in order to reveal original enlightenment.

The commentary explains: Later, in contrast to the revelation of the pure original [enlightenment], for what reason is the name established in relation to that initial enlightenment? It is because of the purity of initial enlightenment.
Because it is identical to the pure fundamental [awakening], the pure fundamental awakening is presented in contrast to the initial awakening (*ādikṣaya*).
Regarding these two types of awakening, what are their characteristics?
The commentary explains: later, when clarifying the two types of perfuming, there are two parts; first, the question: what are the characteristics of the perfuming of the two kinds of pure awakening?
The verse says: (Up to: "There is only one's own virtue. The commentary explains:

The subsequent answer has two parts. First, it concludes the verse regarding purity. Second, it clarifies that the two types of awakening are not defiled by others, yet they are not without mutual perfuming.
Regarding these two purities, as explained in the subsequent treatise, these two pure awakenings may also perfume others.
Because it is a defiled dharma. The Treatise says: [up to] "because it is white and white. The Commentary explains:
The subsequent explanation of the text has two parts: first, an extensive explanation of the two kinds of pure awakening; second, that the defilement of others is not a perfuming agent.
The self-purified is not that which is perfumed, because it lacks the mutual perfuming that depends upon the relativity of defilement and purity;

rather, there are only two purities that mutually perfume one another throughout all stages of cause and fruit. Because the perfuming of purity never ceases, it is called "perfuming in full operation";
and because the perfuming of purity is layered and profound, it is described as "white and white."
"Because the three bodies (up to) transform without differentiation.

The commentary explains that the subsequent citation of evidence regarding "only the perfuming of virtuous qualities" is because the two types of pure enlightened qualities mutually perfume one another;

thus, there is no affliction. Regarding the "perfuming of faultless qualities," since defilement is not a capable perfumer, it is called "faultless perfuming"; it is itself not something that can be perfumed by external purity.
Therefore, it is said that the perfuming of the "virtueless" (amala-vijñāna) involves only the "complete and pervasive turning.

This is because the two types of awakening (the fundamental and the developmental) pervade all fifty-one stages, perfuming them constantly in every thought-moment and turning toward fulfillment; they do not turn stage by stage or in successive portions like the two types of awakening—the defiled and the pure—which progress through the stages and afflictions.
Having already explained the two types of awakening regarding the nature of detachment,
the commentary states that there are two subsequent awakenings— defiled and pure— and first provides a topical outline for the initial section.
This begins with the "initial awakening" (shijue) up to the "initial awakening regarding the nature of detachment."
The commentary states that the subsequent explanation has two parts. First, it clarifies the two types of awakening, which is further divided into two: first, the citation and indication.
What is the meaning of this?

The commentary states that the subsequent section on "displaying" has two parts. First, it raises the question regarding the characteristics of the two types of awakening—defiled and pure—and how they function.
Regarding the meaning of the "intrinsic awakening" (prakṛti-āśraya-jñāna) being "separated from nature":

the commentary states that there are two subsequent explanations. First, it correctly clarifies that the pure fundamental [nature], following conditions, is constantly perfumed by defilement, allowing all defiled phenomena to always find a basis for their abiding.
Second, it clarifies that the pure initial [state], following conditions, is deceived by defilement and only then gives rise to cognition.
Because it cuts off this [delusion], it is called the "initial awakening" (ādi-bodhi) of defilement and purity.
This is because initial awakening reaches and realizes the principle (*tattva*). The commentary explains:

Following the interrogation, there is an explanation regarding the abandonment of delusion. There are two parts: first, the meaning of delusion; second, how initial awakening abandons hindrances and realizes virtues. What is the meaning of delusion? Initial awakening abandons these hindrances and realizes these virtues. What [are they]?
To say that one is "defiled" or "deceived" is because one falsely attributes faults to what is faultless and severs what is real;

it is like seeing a stump at night or flowers in the sky when darkness has ended and cataracts have been removed—what could possibly be seen? Furthermore, to falsely attribute virtues to what is actually devoid of virtue is like a mirror, a lamp, or the moon reflected in water:
when the lamp is extinguished or the moon vanishes, where is the reflection? Thus, the meaning of being "defiled" or "deceived" is made clear herein.
"If that is so... because one reaches the state of non-conceptualization (*amanasikāra*).
The commentary explains: "At the later stage of detachment, one leaves behind delusion and must directly reach the ultimate stage; it is at this time that one attains non-conceptualization."
The two matters concerning the "fulfillment" (pūrṇa) will be demonstrated below.

The commentary states: the subsequent reference to "fulfillment" explains the source of the treatise; having distinguished between awakening and non-awakening, the term "fulfillment" is established, which will be explained extensively in sequence.
The section on the Gate of Determination (*viniścaya-mukha*) has already been explained.
The commentary states that the subsequent detailed exposition of the two types of awakening (*bodhi*) consists of two parts; first is the summary reference.
The root text states [up to]: "because they are of one and the same awakening."

The commentary states: The subsequent exposition has two parts. First, the detailed explanation of the *ādikṣayabodha-viniścaya* (the section on the determination of initial awakening) has two parts. First, the presentation of the root text.
The treatise says: [up to] "establishing the gateway of subsequent awakening."
The commentary states that the subsequent explanation of the text has two parts. First, the establishment of the gates, which further has three sections.
First, the classification [from "the four characteristics" up to] "because they exist as permanent.

The commentary states that the subsequent analysis of the characteristics has two parts. First, the brief presentation of the two gates, which is divided into three. First, the establishment of the gates and their respective applications.

There are two initial sections concerning the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*): first, the two kinds of faults distinguished by the duration of time, which, when investigated in their essence, show no difference;

second, the two kinds of merits, where the meanings in the new version differ but the traced source shows no discrepancy, as both do not transcend taking wisdom and reality (*jñāna-tattva*) as their basis.
"Because [it] follows the awakening (up to) the awakening to non-awakening.

The commentary explains: The gate of subsequent awakening (*pṛṣṭhābhisambodha*) reveals that perfect awakening (*pariniṣpannābhisambodhi*) is identical to ultimate initial awakening (*ādyabhisambodhi*), as they are non-dual and of one characteristic.
Partial awakening (*pradeśābhisambodhi*) reveals the initial awakening at the stage of the cause; it is designated as "awakening" in relation to what precedes it, and in contrast to what follows.
It is called "non-awakening" (*abodha*). Why [is it so]? Because it has existed from the very beginning.

The commentary states: Next, the preceding [section] is examined and analyzed in two parts. First, the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are examined and explained; these are the coarse characteristics, which pertain to long durations.

Because faith reaches the fruit and is able to exhaustively abandon [defilements], the subtle characteristics are established as four types of impermanent marks based on the initial moment of accomplishment, which possesses [all qualities] in a single *kṣaṇa*, and because when faults arise, virtues follow accordingly.
Furthermore, because the virtues that first arise are inferred to exist inherently in the essence, four types of permanent virtuous marks are established. These constitute four sets of four.
Regarding the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), within the context of the five stages (*pañca-avasthā*), it is correctly taught that the four coarse characteristics are abandoned.
However, as long as the faults (*ādīnava*) have not been completely exhausted, both types of the four characteristics of qualities (*guṇa*) still coexist.

Once the ultimate stage—the point where all faults are exhausted—is reached, even the four characteristics of qualities can no longer be established, because all faults are the objects to be remedied (*vipakṣa*), whereas the qualities are their antidotes (*pratipakṣa*).
Because these objects of knowledge are permeated by subsequent afflictions and have not yet reached pure qualities, all meritorious virtues are objects of delusion;

being categorized as objects, they are not included among the faculties of cognition. The virtues that remain unknown pertain generally to both principle and wisdom, while the mind that has not yet known them belongs exclusively to initial enlightenment (*ādikṣānti*).
Below, regarding the relative and the ultimate emptiness, these are designated as "faults" in contrast to their opposites.
When merit awaits impermanence, it is termed "eternally abiding"; yet once faults have been dispelled, merit perishes accordingly. When impermanence has already swept away eternity, what remains?

Because both faults and merits are characterized by the four marks [of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing], they are all empty and non-existent; at that time, there is only a single kind of awakening.
"What is [the reason]... or because it is not yet fully realized?

The commentary explains the subsequent interrogation and resolution regarding "subsequent realization" (*anubodha*). This refers to the fact that there is a distinction between two types of realization: the state of realization during the causal stage and the state of non-realization.
Alternatively, the fifty kinds of partial realization within the causal stage are termed "non-realization" in contrast to the subsequent perfected realization.
Awakening (*bodhi*) is designated as "fulfilled awakening" (*pūrṇa-bodhi*) only at the ultimate stage. This awakening is non-awakening;

when its essential nature is scrutinized, it is solely the initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) reaching its limit and merging with the fundamental [nature], such that there is only a single awakening and no duality.

Subsequently, the analysis of partial awakening (*pradeśa-bodhi*) shows that regardless of which stage one is in, that awakening is called "awakening" only in relation to what precedes it, because there are no longer any defiled dharmas from prior stages to permeate it. Furthermore, regardless of which stage one is in...
Regarding the latter, the term "non-awakening" (a-jñāna) is established because it perfumes subsequent defiled dharmas through the influence of afflictions;

furthermore, it is due to not knowing that the intrinsic nature of the defiled dharmas to be severed is fundamentally pure and truly meritorious. As the treatise below indicates, this perfuming is distinct from both [simultaneous] characteristics.
Next, it is shown that awakening and non-awakening are mutually inclusive and identical in their single flavor. Thus:
This is the meaning.
The characteristics may be observed as explained according to their respective order.

The commentary states that the subsequent reference indicates an exhortation to observe this; it is a preliminary indication intended for those who lecture and investigate, so that they may correlate the text with its corresponding sections.
The meaning is clear.

Herein, from "according to the state of confusion" (至 據亂持故), the commentary explains that the subsequent detailed exposition of the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) has two parts: first, the presentation and enumeration; second, the explanation of those [characteristics] in terms of their non-existence at any time, and so forth.
Because there is a distinction between first severing the characteristic of cessation and subsequently severing the characteristic of arising,

whereas in that state of "sometimes," the subtle arises first and the coarse ceases later; since there is no temporal distinction, it is based on the fact that through the delusion of ignorance regarding the true realm (*dharmadhātu*),
all four characteristics are simultaneously established at once.
"Simultaneous existence" (*sahabhū*) [up to] "grossness and subtlety," thus four.

The commentary states: the subsequent detailed expansion of the sequence has two parts. First, the sequence of simultaneous existence, which further has two parts. First, the general explanation, which further has two parts:

first, the question-and-answer regarding simultaneous existence; [it is shown that] the subtle characteristic of arising comes first, and the gross characteristic of cessation comes later, explaining their simultaneity at once.
The coarse and subtle explanations of the sequence are intended merely to encompass both the preceding and succeeding moments simultaneously.
Herein, [from "to" (至)] there are four characteristics in each instance.

The commentary states: the subsequent inquiry and explanation concern what is grasped simultaneously; at one time, ignorance perfumes the True [Mind], and in a single thought-moment, all four [characteristics] are complete.
Delusion conceals the true nature and obscures the pure mind, causing one to wander through birth and death without end.
Why is this so? What are its characteristics?

The commentary explains that these will be clarified separately later; first, regarding the characteristic of arising, there are four aspects. Second, first, the four characteristics are raised collectively; next, the question concerning arising.
What are the characteristics of these four types of meanings?
The verse says: "Because it establishes the initial arising. The commentary explains:
Subsequently, by specifically addressing the characteristic of arising, it answers that the ignorance-infused mind produces the three subtle marks; [these] function independently.

The subtle functioning arising from the ignorance of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-avidyā*) acts alone, while the subtle functioning arising from the fundamental awakening (*prakṛti-pratibhāsa*) acts in conjunction with it;

because these two functions are distinct, they are called "acting alone" and "acting in conjunction. The aspect of movement consists of grasping that movement which arises through the harmony and combination of karma and conditions.
If one is separated from the movement of karma and conditions, there is no movement in conjunction, just as there are no waves when wind and water are absent.

The Dharma and the analogy each possess three aspects; these three first arise, and are thus called the "characteristic of arising" (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*). Among the three subtle [states], this corresponds to the first subtle state;

among the eleven mental states, it corresponds to the "characteristic of karma" (*karma-lakṣaṇa*) within the "consciousness of karma" (*karma-vijñāna*). Among the five types of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), it is the characteristic of arising;
among the six types of defiled states, it is the "karma" within the "non-associated [conditioned] phenomena" (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
"Because the abiding characteristic (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*) does not extend to the coarse divisions. The commentary explains:

Among the two abiding characteristics, it refers to the latter of the three subtle [characteristics]; among the six coarse [characteristics], it refers to the first; among the twenty-one mental factors, it refers to the latter eight;

and among the six kinds of defilements, it refers to the middle four. The meaning of "abiding" (*sthiti*) in these four types of abiding characteristics is distinct: they function as the characteristic of abiding (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*).
The sustaining power that perceives the perfuming of the mind-consciousness (*manovijñāna*) sustains the manifestation of superior and inferior signs;

the perfuming of the material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) sustains the signs of superior and inferior wisdom; and the perfuming of the defiled phenomena of discrimination sustains the six gradual stages that obstruct the second through the seventh grounds.
This is because it does not grasp the six coarse states or the six types of defilement; rather, its characteristic is the continuity that sustains the objective consciousness (*vastu-vijñāna*).

Because the defilements are uninterrupted, although the characteristics of the four abodes (catuḥ-vihāra) internally contain both coarse and subtle aspects, they are further subdivided in relation to their distinct modes of cessation.

Furthermore, within the *vastu-vijñāna* (object-consciousness), six are manifest while seven are latent; by distinguishing the coarse from the subtle, that which consists solely of attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) is designated as the subtle subdivision.
"Because of arising attachment to different characteristics (*vilakṣaṇa*).

The commentary explains: Among the three different characteristics and the six coarse [defilements], the first two within the internal [set] and the first one within the six defilements—if one grasps the characteristic of apprehension (*udgraha-lakṣaṇa*), it is established as a name based on the cognitive activity of the subject (*ālambaka*).
Because it is the very characteristic that is grasped, it is said to "become different by itself" (*svayaṃ vilakṣaṇaṃ bhavati*) through its own differentiation.

Based on various distinct characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), one gives rise to various attachments; because the subjective perceiver differs from itself, it is called the "characteristic of difference" (*vilakṣaṇa*).

The "characteristic of naming" (*nāmalakṣaṇa*) refers to establishing names for the objects of perception; the characteristic that is identified as such is called the "characteristic of difference," meaning that ordinary fools give rise to attachment based on names, and this is so named because of the differences among the objects of perception. These two—[the characteristic of difference and the characteristic of naming]—are [as follows].

The designation "person-grasping" (pudgala-grāha) is established based on the predominance of either the agent or the object; according to the *Bhadramitra-ṭīkā*, grasping (*grāha*) refers to that which is innate (*sahaja*), while the conceptualization of names (*nāma-vikalpa*) belongs to the discriminative (*parikalpita*).
It is called the "characteristic of cessation" (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) because it reaches the state of cessation.

The commentary states: The karma produced by the four characteristics of cessation and the fruit it summons destroy prior grasping and the conceptualization of names, thereby causing one to undergo suffering;
or, at the time of receiving the fruit, they extinguish various virtues; or, at the time of initiating karma, they impair innate goodness.
Because the meaning of "cessation" is intended to be shown as mutually pervasive, the sequence of cause and effect is presented here in reverse order.
Having already explained simultaneous existence, we shall now explain sequential existence.
The commentary states: regarding the two types of sequential order—prior and posterior—the first provides a summary indication.
What are their characteristics?
The commentary states that the subsequent explanation has two parts. First is the question.
The verse says: [up to] "the differences in increase and decrease.
The commentary states that the subsequent answer has two parts. First is the verse which, in response to the treatise, explains the sequence of the time of abandonment from cessation to arising.
First coarse and later subtle; because the fruits of self-confidence vary according to the increase or decrease of wisdom, the remedies differ.

Regarding this meaning [up to] the difference in increase and decrease, the commentary explains that the subsequent assignment of stages involves the presence or absence of the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*), because those in the stage of the ten faiths eliminate the characteristic of cessation, whereas those in the stage of the three worthies (*trikalyāṇapudgala*)...

Because those in the first nine stages counteract the characteristic of difference (*visadṛśa-lakṣaṇa*), those on the ten stages counteract the characteristic of abiding (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*), and those at the stage of the fulfillment of the coarse division of arising counteract the subtle division;
thus, at the point where the four characteristics are exhausted, there is ultimate purity (*atyanta-viśuddhi*).
The section on sequential explanation has already been discussed.
The commentary states that the subsequent section on sequential explanation has two parts; first is the summary reference:
based on those four characteristics, up to the stage where the fruit is perfected.

The commentary states that the subsequent explanation has two parts. First, the definitive analysis of the five stages, which itself has two parts. First, the brief classification and discussion, which further has two parts.
First, the headings, inquiries, and enumeration of the stages; the differentiation of the stages is established according to the characteristics of what is to be abandoned.
Regarding the statement "In the first four [positions]... it explains the contemplation of association" (*yogānupassanā*):

the commentary explains that the Master [Vasubandhu], in his treatise on the varying number of factors (*vastu*) in the subsequent [positions], instructs students to clearly remember the four and three [factors] as they correspond to the respective textual passages.
The first [stage] is named "The Awakened One" (*buddha*).

The commentary explains that, based on the subsequent stages, there is a detailed exposition of five [categories], the first of which is the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*). Within this, there are four aspects:

first, the practitioner who is able to cultivate; the bodhisattva of the ten faiths has not yet entered the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), and is therefore called an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), yet they have already emerged [from the mundane].
Those of false resolve are also called "awakened ones" because they perceive the meaning of the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of awakening.
The commentary states: regarding the two causes for practice, before entering the stage of faith, one neither knows nor awakens to the fact that karma is performed and its fruits are received.
This is a great calamity: by creating various nets of karma, one summons the wheel of suffering for each and every act; the five destinies ceaselessly revolve and the four modes of birth never rest.

Now that you have encountered a virtuous friend, this is a pure and excellent condition for purification. You must pull yourself from the dense forest of false views and enter the stage of faith in merit.
Karma is the seed of suffering and its fruit is a source of poison; though there may be lingering calamities, they ultimately possess no reality.
Because one desires to manifest the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*) and is able to comprehend the cessation of defilements, subsequently giving rise to a mind that correctly restrains evil,
this is designated as the characteristic of the cause of practice. Thus, one is able to bring [the mind] to rest so that it does not arise [again].

The commentary states: Regarding the characteristics of the cause and effect of the three practices, there are two interpretations. First, it says "therefore" (*ataḥ*), which signifies the sense of deliberate mental attention (*manasikāra*).
When faith first arises, the path of remediation is extremely weak; this is the gateway for upward transformation. It is the path that leaves this shore.

If one encounters laxity, one will again fall back into the influence of the lower stages; however, if one remains earnest, one may suddenly transcend to the rank of a noble one (*ārya*). Thus, it is said "therefore."
The capacity [of the practitioner] lies in this very point. Second, it is said that "so" (*yī*) signifies the sense of cause and condition;

because one previously failed to awaken, one constantly cultivated evil conditions, whereas subsequently, through deep realization, one forever engages in pure deeds (*śukla-karman*). Thus, one feels remorse for past errors and fears further evil, remaining untainted by transgressions committed by others;
one feels shame before the worthy and exalted, ensuring that one does not personally incur fault or blame. This latter meaning explains the underlying intention (*abhiprāya*).
Regarding the discussion of cause and effect herein: when prior awakening ceases and one seeks its severance, this is termed the "cause of practice";
when one stops evil so that it does not arise, this is designated as the "result.
Although [this process] involves the mutual perfuming and separation of the two aspects...

The commentary states: Regarding the four types of perfuming (*vāsanā*) and their separation from the dual characteristics, there are two parts. First, citing the terms "perfuming" and "separation" to explain the meaning of "enlightened awareness" (*bodhi*);
second, citing the term "perfuming together with" (*saha-vāsanā*) to explain "non-enlightened unawareness" (*abodhi*).
That is to say, [the text] speaks of "perfuming and separation" because of these reasons.
The commentary states that there are four subsequent explanations: first, knowing the defects and their remedies;

because one knows that the characteristics of cessation are in fact defects, one gives rise to the bodhicitta and brings about the cessation of phenomena, so that subsequent thoughts do not arise; this is called "perfuming detachment."
Regarding the passage from the "Chapter on the Characteristics of Cessation" (to the point where it says):

"Therefore, it is said that perfuming and co-arising [are simultaneous]. The commentary explains: Although the two delusions regarding virtue have ceased once awakening has been attained, because perfuming and co-arising remain distinct from what has not yet been awakened, one still fails to realize through this co-arising of perfuming that the fundamental nature of the characteristics of cessation is originally pure; this is truly the merit [of the teaching].
Virtue. Regarding this [passage] up to "in the tenth stage," the commentary states:
although the three streams reach the tenth stage and are termed "awakening," they merely serve as antidotes for the purpose of perfuming and abandoning [the afflictions].
The four characteristics of the faults (*ādīnava*) are precisely this non-awakening (*abodhi*); these manifest simultaneously with their perfuming (*vāsanā*), yet they remain uncomprehended.

The four characteristics of the merits (*guṇa*) correspond to this: according to this treatise, they refer to the stage of the causal state (*hetu-bhūmi*). Although awakening has been partially attained, subsequent afflictions continue to perfume [the mind] and remain concurrent with it; thus, one does not yet harmonize with original awakening (*mūla-awakening*).

Only upon reaching full awakening, when there is no longer the perfuming of subsequent afflictions, does one realize that the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the four characteristics is pure and that they have always been, in reality, merits.
The four characteristics of virtue and the afflictions of those characteristics are exhausted; the portion of the characteristics of virtue is fulfilled and awakening vanishes.

At that time, there is only a single awakening because it functions as such. Therefore, the subsequent treatise states: "In reality, there is no distinction between a superior transformation and gradual succession, nor is there a limit of perfect culmination, because one accords with the non-dual, single-characteristic awakening. Thus, although this treatise refers to it by the name "awakening," [it is so designated only conventionally].

This means that non-awakening (a-vijñapti) flows down to the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), with the sole exception of the fruit-stage (*phala-avasthā*), because there is no longer the coexistence of perfuming (*vāsanā*) and [the seeds].
Furthermore, it is because [this stage] is of a single flavor (*eka-rasa*).

The commentary states: "The fourth [point] reveals that the essence is of a single flavor. This is said for fear that people might falsely identify this non-awakening within [the stages] as being either the root or the branches.
Because ignorance is non-awakening, it is shown in detail that awakening and non-awakening are profoundly interpenetrated in a single flavor.

This [state] is called "initial awakening" (śikṣābodhi) in contrast to what precedes it, because it has overcome the afflictions of non-awakening; yet it is called "non-awakening" in contrast to what follows it, because it still possesses the delusions regarding meritorious qualities.
It is like gold mixed with ore: when compared to the coarse sand and ore that have been partially removed, although it is called "gold," it still retains its impurities.
Because there are still fine sand-like mineral ores remaining, it is still called "ore-gold"; yet the gold extracted from the ore and the gold remaining in the ore are not two different entities.
Likewise, within the state of phenomena, the awakening that is free from delusion and the awakening that remains amidst delusion are of one and the same flavor.
"Because it is the ocean of the second stage. The commentary explains:

"The two or three noble stages have four [categories]: first, those who are practitioners heading toward [the goal]; second, those of the Two Vehicles belonging to the group of the wrongly fixed (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*), because they do not seek bodhi and lack the great mind (*mahācitta*);
now, we take the wisdom of the empty contemplation (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā-jñāna*) of those of the Two Vehicles as being identical [to that of the Bodhisattvas]."

Because they belong to the stage of the Three Worthies (*trayaḥ pūrvamārga*), they are called "similar" (*pratirūpa*). Within the stage of the Three Worthies indicated by this treatise, there is the grasping and conceptualization of names without distinction between priority or sequence, nor between seed and manifestation.
These general categories are divided into ninety parts. Obstacles are countered by the path, with the number of factors being equal;
through comparative observation, the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) stages of the wisdom realizing the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) are accomplished part by part at each stage.

One attains mastery such that there is no longer any doubt or fear regarding the various afflictions to be abandoned. Alternatively, when a practitioner reaches the stage of Dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) and the tenth "Emerging Mind," they finally exhaust all grasping at the characteristics of persons;
as the realization of person-emptiness (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) becomes untainted (*anāsrava*), one reaches the ultimate stage of the Worthy One (*ārya*) and is free from all doubt and fear.
According to the system of Master Xianshou, this is explained in terms of demarcating the stages by manifesting them through the afflictions and thereby severing those afflictions.

Those in the stage of the Gate-Worthy (Śaikṣa) merely suppress the active manifestations of coarse afflictions; when entering the Path of Seeing (Darśanamārga), they are able to suddenly sever their seeds.

This does not contradict the meaning previously discussed in this treatise. Because the power of the Path is sovereign, one may sever [afflictions] while leaving some behind without obstruction, for the sake of benefiting oneself and others;
thus, it is necessary to leave some behind. Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* says: "If one does not sever the higher mental states, one is no different from an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). If...

Leaving the seeds intact means that this is not different from the Two Vehicles; it also accords with the aforementioned treatise in that it counteracts and suddenly severs the four abodes of views (*dṛṣṭi-vāsa*).
Furthermore, it reveals that both vehicles contain the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*);

when the spiritual consciousness within the aggregates is fully realized, one ultimately cultivates the causes of the myriad practices and attains the fruit of the three bodies (*trikāya*), finally flowing into the ocean of *samyak-prajñā*.
"Awakening to [the distinction] up to awakening to the difference in mindfulness.
The commentary explains: the two causes for the practice of cultivation refer to the conceptualization of names and the subsequent perfuming of the grasping of various objects;

by taking these as objective conditions, one grasps them, and this assistance to the conceptualization of names results in the individual discrimination of the characteristics of words, both superior and inferior.

As these powers mutually permeate one another, every person’s discursive thought further increases their grasping at "I" and "mine," causing them to rise and fall within the three realms and appear and disappear among the four modes of birth; since they do not cultivate through such permeation, where can this cease?

Now, as the initial awakening to the emptiness of persons arises, the skillful means for attaining the emptiness of phenomena also manifests before one, whereby one comes to know that the mind of original awakening was merely in a state of sleep.
In the great night of ignorance, one dreams of diverse appearances and is deluded regarding the reality of dharmas; wishing to eliminate these entanglements, one must rely on the path of cultivation.

By gradually giving rise to the awakening of cultivation and progressively shattering the mind of delusion, one realizes that the dream of discursive thought arises in vain and gives way to a semblance of true awakening.
As this sublime practice is thus set in motion, it is called "cultivation" (*pratipatti*). This is the cause.
"Because mindfulness is free from [even] the most extreme joy. The commentary explains:
Through the three modes of practice, cause and effect mutually depend on one another; by means of prior realization, right mindfulness is induced.

When the clarity of right mindfulness arises, the darkness of divergent characteristics (*vilakṣaṇa*) subsides. Next, the reason for this is stated: Why is it that as soon as right mindfulness arises, it causes divergent characteristics to be swiftly [eliminated]?

Cessation (*nirodha*) is defined by the presence of two types of discrimination within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*): the coarse and the subtle. The coarse refers to afflictions such as greed and hatred that arise in dependence on favorable or unfavorable objects;

these constitute the afflictive obscuration (*kleśāvaraṇa*), being comprised of the aspect of grasping at and conceptualizing names. The subtle refers to the habitual flow of the clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), which constitutes the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
This is comprised of the aspect of continuity (*anubandha-lakṣaṇa*), which is subsumed under the aspect of abiding (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*); it need not be discussed separately.

Regarding the characteristic of wisdom: because it is co-emergent with that [mind], it now serves merely as an antidote to coarse greed, hatred, and so forth, rather than being a subtle attachment to dharmas;
thus, when right mindfulness arises, the characteristic of differentiation is extinguished, and its characteristic of continuity is abandoned at the first stage (*bhūmi*).
Therefore, it is called "cognition resembling [the object] up to [the limit].
The commentary states: "The four types of perfuming are free from co-arising; this correctly concludes the name of cognition while simultaneously clarifying its freedom from co-arising.
Because the explanation is not detailed, it says, "along with 'coarse' (cū). The character *cū* (麤) is identical to the character *chien* (兼). Taking *cū* as *chien* is appropriate in meaning.

The well-perfumed and the perfumed-free are both to be understood as before. Similarity between different categories is established through analogy based on partial resemblance, while similarity within the same category is established through inference based on complete resemblance.
This extends up to the third [stage], the Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body.
The commentary states: Regarding the three sets of nine stages, there are four [categories]. First, those practitioners who are progressing toward the final two *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.

Second, those in the first nine stages whose true suchness (*tathatā*) constitutes their body and whose prajñā constitutes their mind; they have already emerged from the defilements and burdens of the two kinds of attachment to dharmas, and whether in body or mind, they are pure and luminous.
Third, those for whom the bonds and obstructions of the two subtle ālayas are entirely severed, both with respect to objects and with respect to gnosis.
Having emerged from the fetters of defilement through unimpeded mastery, and because wisdom and means are fused, one is named a Bodhisattva of the Dharmakāya.
This accords well with the aforementioned treatise; practicing according to reality and taking refuge in the Saṃgha of the Ten Stages is thus clearly understood.
"Awakening up to awakening in the station of mindfulness.

The commentary explains: regarding the two causal characteristics of practice prior to entering the [bodhisattva] stages, the four types of abiding characteristics constantly give rise to attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*).

Consequently, original awakening (*mūlapratyavekṣā*) remains dormant within the dream-like state of the characteristic of dwelling in ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*), such that there is no realization. This is the dawn of initial awakening (*ādikṣānti*).
Once the wheel has emerged, the characteristics of abiding and the dreams of the night are both eliminated; light and darkness, being contradictory, cannot function simultaneously.
Furthermore, initial awakening (*ādikṣaya*) is the nature of correct non-discrimination, while the characteristic of abiding is the state of confusion with discrimination.

Since correctness and confusion are contradictory and existence and non-existence do not coexist, when the path of abandonment manifests, one must first apply effort toward the mindfulness of awakening; this is called "cultivation."
Cause. Contemplating that [each] is devoid of a single characteristic.

The commentary states: the three modes of practice arise from the causal characteristics; through prior awakening and understanding, right mindfulness is induced, and as soon as right mindfulness arises...

The characteristic of abiding (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*) is extinguished next; the reason for its presentation here is the fear that this characteristic of abiding might be confused with the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, because the deluded conceptualization regarding abiding in contrast to arising is extremely coarse and heavy, among the four characteristics of abiding, the characteristic of continuity (*prabandha-lakṣaṇa*) constitutes a specific obstacle to one type of wisdom—the wisdom of severing [afflictions] in the Stage of Extreme Joy (*parama-pramuditā*)—which is severed progressively from the second through the seventh stages according to each respective stage.

"Transcending the three realms of existence" refers to the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), meaning that one is able to transcend the three realms of existence; for this reason, this stage is established with the name "Far-Reaching" (*dūraṃgamā*).
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that it "surpasses the worldly path and the path of the two vehicles. Here, "transcending the three realms of existence" means transcending the world.
This treatise omits the mention of surpassing the two vehicles. The eighth stage (*bhūmi*) abandons the manifest [afflictions], while the ninth stage abandons...
They are so named because they function as antidotes to each other in their respective order.
[The phrase] "up to not having emerged" is explained as follows:

the four perfumings (*vāsanā*) are free from both characteristics; this correctly binds the realization of awakening, and the name also simultaneously reveals the freedom from both types of pursuit. This is the detailed explanation.
Regarding the perfuming of the simultaneous characteristics: because the subtle thought of the karmic characteristic has not yet been transcended, these delusions still exist;

thus, the perfuming follows partial awakening, leading to a lack of awareness of the four characteristics of merit. The sequential and simultaneous perfuming of these four characteristics should be understood by analogy with this.
The fourth [section] extends to the path of non-antidote (*apratipakṣa-mārga*).
The commentary states: the stage of fulfillment of the four causes and the stage of fulfillment of the five fruits are combined and divided into two.

First, the two persons are combined to explain that within the exhaustion of the stages (*bhūmi-kṣaya*), the exhaustion of the stage of training (*śaikṣa-bhūmi*) is called the fulfillment of the cause, while the attainment of the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) is called the fulfillment of the fruit.
The perfection of causes and the perfection of the abandonment of obstacles eliminate a portion of the coarse afflictions associated with the aspect of movement in conjunction;

the perfection of results eliminates the aspect of karma acting alone as well as the great ignorance. According to the subsequent treatise, it is also indicated that a portion of the subtle afflictions—the obstacles to the result—are eliminated.

These include the aspect of movement in conjunction, the aspect of following [the object] acting alone, and the karmic function of primordial awareness (*mūlabodhi*). Since this is not an intrinsic defilement, there is no path capable of severing it.
Question: Since these belong to the category of the six defilements and the five conditioned states (*saṃskṛta*), how can they be said to be severed? Answer:
Once ignorance is severed, fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) does not arise; from this perspective, non-arising is also described as "severance.

However, with respect to what has already been activated previously, when the solitary power [of the mind] and its conforming characteristics perish along with karma, this is not a severance of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
From here below (up to) "the one who is perfected.
The commentary states: regarding the separate explanation of the latter two perfections, there are two parts;
first, a general indication, which fulfills [the requirements] and designates that person.

The commentary states: Regarding the subsequent detailed analysis, there are two parts. First, concerning the fulfillment of the causes, there are two types of persons at the stage of cause-fulfillment who possess certainty:
first, the *upāya-vajra*, which corresponds to the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), as indicated by the preceding phrase of the treatise;

second, the *mūla-vajra*, which corresponds to the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), as indicated by the following phrase of the treatise. Alternatively, a single moment of mental application (*ekakṣaṇa-samprayukta*) may also constitute the path of preparation.

The fulfillment of the practice of the Path through the single-moment correspondence constitutes the path of uninterrupted continuity (*ānantarya-mārga*). By citing the path that has arisen, it reveals the person who gives rise to it.

Furthermore, these two phrases may also implicitly contain the latter three matters: the meditative concentration of skillful means (*upāya-samādhi*) as the causal characteristic of cultivation, and the fundamental meditative concentration (*maula-samādhi*) as the resultant characteristic of the practice.
Since it is already granted that the characteristics of counteracting and simultaneous movement both belong to the category of perfuming (*vāsanā*).

Even when separated from [the coarse afflictions], there still remain subtle delusions and the permeation of great ignorance; furthermore, since these permeations coexist, they do not contradict the aforementioned treatise, as each possesses four causes.
This is because the awakened mind reaches the realization of non-arising.
The commentary states: Regarding the fulfillment of the subsequent fruit, there are two aspects; first, the perfection of the initial fruit. There are four characteristics of its complete practice:

(1) possessing the three marks of clarity, which identifies the person by citing the path—that is, one who is capable of fulfillment; (2) the characteristic of counteractive practice, wherein wisdom arises and delusions perish;

(3) bringing the path of liberation to ultimate completion; and (4) the manifestation of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), through which one attains universal penetration such that none can equal it.
When the characteristics of karma and ignorance no longer exist, there is an equality that is empty and devoid of marks; how could there be any thought?
By remaining far removed from inferior states and fulfilling the ultimate mark, one realizes that the four marks are fundamentally pure and are in truth meritorious virtues.
Because one attains the vision of the nature of the mind by leaving behind subtle thoughts, one reaches the realization of non-arising.
"Therefore, [up to] 'the fruit of Buddhahood is without thought.
The commentary explains: regarding the two proofs for being free from the two kinds of thought, there are two parts. First, it reveals the absence of deluded thought:

when the practitioner reaches the stage of the fruit of Buddhahood at the time of the Path of Liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), they are free from the thought of ignorance and the subtle marks of karmic activity at the stage of the Path of Ultimate Liberation (*atyanta-vimukti-mārga*).
Because they do not coexist, it is said that the fruit of Buddhahood is without thought; one should know that such a person is proceeding toward the stage of a Buddha.
If there is no [attainment], one should examine this with care.
The commentary states: It is explained later that possessing right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) means being far removed from false thoughts and not falling into mere emptiness or non-existence.
When right mindfulness is conjoined with the ten virtues and functions simultaneously within the first moment of the path of supreme liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), it is termed "right mindfulness."

Furthermore, regarding the passage from "Moreover, as for the arising of the mind" up to "causing the production of resolute conviction," the commentary explains that there are two [parts] to the removal of doubt and the production of understanding:
first, the citation and indication, which states: "There are [those who]... because of such doubts."
The commentary states that there are two parts to the subsequent explanation. First, it sets forth the doubt:

regarding the fundamental awakened wisdom (*mūla-awakening*) at the point of attaining the fruit, one wonders whether its subtle aspect of arising should be known as conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

If it were known to exist, then within the state of Buddhahood it would not be "non-conceptual" (*amala-vikalpa*), because the subtle conceptuality of the aspect of arising would still be present. If it were known to be non-existent, then the fruit of Buddhahood would be complete...
If awakening were to exist, it could not do so; for in the absence of an initial thought, against what could awakening be established?
Now, [the author] provides his own explanation (extending to the point where he says) "one merely knows the initial characteristic.

The commentary states: This subsequent general response is that Māng (Aśvaghoṣa) generally explains that the initial characteristic of the object of knowledge is originally empty by nature, and that which knows it...

The Dharma of initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) is naturally such that it does not give rise to the mind and its objects; since from the beginning there was nothing, what "beginning" could be known? Now, when we speak of "knowing," it is to reveal the absence of thought.

Although the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is profoundly still and originally transcends both the perceiving subject and the perceived object, true awakening is spiritually luminous, realizing the state where there is neither mind nor object.
It merely brushes away the subtle marks of duality; what obstacle could hinder one’s thorough penetration into this non-duality?
The awakening to the non-existence of these two is itself ultimate awakening; it is neither a mere emptiness nor a manifestation of nothingness, for it is not a state of annihilation.
Based on this principle, one knows the initial characteristic.
Therefore, [up to] it is called "Buddha."
The commentary states: The fourfold establishment of non-thought (amanasikāra) mentions sentient beings as possessing thought and reveals the Buddhas as being without thought;
although the phrasing employs inverse illustration (*pratiloma*), the intent is to provide a direct clarification (*anuloma*).
This continues until the section on "pervasive perfection."
The commentary states that the subsequent section on the perfection of the object of *prstha-abhisambodhi* has two parts;
first, the presentation of the headings, which says: "As for the Greatly Awakened One... [up to] ...because of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing.

The commentary further explains that the subsequent section on the exposition has two parts; first, the analysis of the all-pervasive nature of the object, wherein the *prstha-abhisambodhi* of the Buddha-fruit universally knows the direction of [all phenomena].

Birth merely arises based on the single mind and evolves into the four characteristics. Why? Because it is devoid of conceptualization (*manasikāra*) and so forth. The commentary explains that there are three parts to the subsequent explanation establishing this reason: first, the interrogation; second, the knowledge that reveals [the state]; and third, the manifestation that the Buddha is devoid of the four characteristics. What is the reason? Because he is without conceptualization and so forth. Thus it is said: "Because he is without conceptualization and so forth.
