Initial enlightenment (ādi-bodhi) eliminates delusions because it is first [in sequence] and immeasurable."

The commentary states that there are four subsequent specific distinctions: first, the analogy of the wood, such as the *ariḷada* (here translated as "dragon-ancient wood"), which illustrates the five matters—profound depth and so forth—contained within ignorance (*avidyā*) within the Dharma;
this corresponds to the primary meaning. The "branches and tips" and "lack of awakening" correspond to the third meaning.
The two characters for "delusion" (*mohu*) correspond to the third meaning, and the two characters for "faults" (*guo-shi*) correspond to [the fourth].

Because the fourth meaning is immeasurable, it is assigned to the fifth meaning; alternatively, all [meanings] from the second downward may be applied collectively to the latter four, because of the presence or absence of fundamental enlightenment (mūla-bodhi).
The commentary states: The two similes of fire illustrate seven dharmas; these seven are visible in the text.
Regarding the third [simile], it is because there is likewise no skillful means (*upāya*).
The commentary states: The simile of the three people illustrates the *Bhāradvāja-tīrthika*, which is translated here as "one who possesses skillful means."
*Śyātala* means "lack of skillful means. A person possessing skillful means is well-acquainted with five matters and is thus able to obtain fire;
a person lacking skillful means, being unacquainted with these five matters, will ultimately not obtain fire.

Within the Dharma, there must likewise be a person possessing skillful means who fully understands five matters, and such a person can immediately realize the fruit: first, knowing the nature of emergence and perceiving defilement.
1. Know that the Dharma is like wood; 2. know that the mind and wisdom for its skillful practice are like a drill; 3. know the timing for sudden awakening and gradual cultivation;
4. know the location where body and mind reside; 5. know the sequence of faith in the fruits of the noble ones.
Those who possess skillful means will fully attain the state of profound stillness, whereas those lacking expedient means will ultimately find it difficult to achieve the fruit.
Fourth, [it is] because of the single-pointedness of mind.
The commentary states: within the four similes of burning, three types of analogies can be observed.
Having already explained the second [point], namely the specific explanation.
The commentary states that the subsequent combined exposition has two parts. First, the summary introduction that categorizes the sections.
Regarding the term "general exposition" (up to the point where it says): "...sentient beings are likewise.
The commentary further states that the subsequent analysis of characteristics according to the categories has two parts, beginning with the general exposition category.
Regarding the "separate exposition" (up to) the "gate of complete fulfillment":
the commentary states that the subsequent gate of separate exposition has two parts. First is the "gate of explaining the intent and opening [the discussion]":
because if conditions are lacking, such a state cannot possibly exist.
The commentary explains that there are three sections based on the subsequent gates of reliance. First, regarding the gate of the single cause due to the deficiency of conditions:
although fire exists within wood, if it has long been dormant and one does not encounter the necessary means, it will ultimately be difficult to obtain the fire.

Likewise, although the Buddha-nature has long been contained within the storehouse of ignorance, if one does not engage in practice, one cannot attain Buddhahood; the rules for such practice must rely upon the instruction and transmission of teachers and friends.
One attains the realization of the Buddha-way by relying on conditions to initiate practice.
This is because, due to the deficiency of causes, one does not yet seek nirvana.
The commentary states: Next is the "gate of the deficiency of single conditions. Even if fire-nature is originally absent within wood, although the conditions may be present...
Just as one will ultimately never obtain fire [without fuel], if a person has no Buddha-nature inherently within their mind, they will never attain Buddhahood despite possessing complete practice;
this meaning is a provisional statement that people lack Buddha-nature because, being deficient in the cause, they ultimately do not become Buddhas.

This correctly reveals the tenet of our school: how could there be any sentient being who does not possess Buddha-nature? It is only because their obstructions are thick and the power of internal permeation is weak.
Furthermore, since it is said that the deficiency in causes does not mean they are actually non-existent, the *Mūla-śāstra* states:

"Although the power of conditions exists, the internal pure dharmas have not yet acquired the power of perfuming. This serves as proof. Since it says they "have not yet [arisen]," it does not mean they lack an original nature.
"Because it serves as the causal condition for proceeding toward the path to nirvāṇa.

The commentary explains: "In the gateway of the fulfillment of subsequent conditions, just as wood possesses the nature of fire and, upon encountering the condition of drilling, causes the fire to emerge and burn the wood until nothing remains;
so too, if sentient beings have the internal permeation of original enlightenment (prakṛti-āśraya) and further encounter teachers and friends who provide instruction,"

With external assistance, one cultivates the causes of the hundred practices to achieve the fruit of the ten thousand virtues; the three types of knowledge are perfected and the four virtues are fully endowed.
Having already explained [the general overview] up to this point, the second part is the specific explanation.
The commentary states that the subsequent section on the "Gate of Manifesting Understanding through Detailed Exposition" has two parts: first, the summary that introduces and divides the sections.
Regarding the general exposition (up to): "...by the power of external conditions.
The commentary states that there are two parts to the subsequent section, which clarifies the meaning through the gateway of the basis (*āśraya*). First is the gateway of the general exposition.

Within this, the "subjective cognizer" (*ālambaka*) refers to the *nirmāṇakāya* and *sambhogakāya*, which belong to the function of perfuming (*vāsana*). This corresponds in meaning to the inconceivable activity of original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*), which manifests various objective realms and draws [beings] [toward it].
The mastery of the faculties should be uninterrupted; that which is able to act as a distinguished condition for birth is called the "function of the perceiving subject" (*ālambaka-vyāpāra*).
As for the term "perfuming" (*vāsanā*), it refers to the person. Furthermore, it is said that the "object of perception" (*ālambana*) consists of all realms of sentient beings emanated by the Buddha.
The original treatise also states that the power of external conditions is mentioned here in accordance with the flow of the text and its terminology; that is what it means.
Because it is the function of the fundamental awakening that serves as the object of cognition, this passage clarifies the realm of sentient beings as its objective support;
thus, the intent of the treatise is to reveal that the perfuming of function—the responsive and transformational bodies—constantly acts as an external conditioning force for sentient beings.

Setting aside the detailed explanation [from] "in the middle" (up to) "because of equal conditions," the commentary states that the subsequent section on the detailed exposition has two parts. First, the classification of the gates belongs to the original [text]:
by means of discernment, one understands specific conditions; by means of non-discernment, one understands equal conditions.

Regarding the phrase "the object-referent (*ālambana*) that is reached," the commentary explains that there are two parts to the subsequent analysis of characteristics according to their categories. First, there is the discernment of the object, which has three parts. First, regarding the distinction between the subject that perceives (*ālambaka*) and the object perceived (*ālambana*), there are two parts; first, the classification.
"Because it is able to serve as a condition (ālambana) [up to] the attainment of benefit.

The commentary explains that this subsequently demonstrates how the person who acts as the condition—beginning from the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment (cittotpāda) and ending with the state of a Tathāgata—is able to act as this condition to attract and gather those whose faculties are suitable.
Their objective referent (ālambana-viṣaya) is the faculties of those to be converted, namely, those of the group fixed in error (mithyātva-niyata-rāśi) and...
Because the indeterminate group (*aniyata-rāśi*) may also transform those in the fixed group (*niyata-rāśi*), it possesses the capacity to take persons as objects;
thus, the correlation between the objects of perception and the textual exegesis can be understood through reflection. From this point onward, up to [the section on] their distinctions...
The commentary states: Next, regarding those who have already matured and those who have not yet matured, there are two types of inducement;
first is the classification, which refers to sentient beings [who will attain liberation] after a long period of time.
The commentary states: This subsequently demonstrates [the meaning].

From this point downward, up to the "condition for increasing the fruit" (*phalavardhana-pratyaya*), the commentary explains that there are two distinct categories regarding the differentiation of distant and proximate causes and effects. First is the classification [of the conditions].
Regarding the "condition for increasing the cause" (*hetuvardhana-pratyaya*), it extends up to the "condition for receiving the path" (*mārga-lābha-pratyaya*).

The commentary states: The subsequent passage demonstrates that there is a difference in the speed [of attainment] between the two conditions—the distant and the near—because both increase the causes for the myriad practices and together bring about the long-term fruition of the myriad virtues.
This concludes the explanation of the second point, which is distinct [from the preceding].
The commentary states: Regarding the two subsequent conditions for non-discrimination, first is the summary that links the sections and establishes their divisions.
Within the general exposition, up to the phrase "because one never abandons it," the commentary states:

regarding the two subsequent explanations of characteristics according to the gates, first is the general exposition of the gates, which has three parts; the first is the cultivation of loving-kindness and vows.
It gives rise to the objective realm of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, which extends vertically through the three periods of time and encompasses horizontally the ten directions,
constantly perfuming the roots of goodness of sentient beings so that they may increase;
this is because their wisdom of identical essence (samatā-jñāna) reaches everywhere without exception.

The commentary states: Next, regarding the "True Benefactor" (Saccakārī), the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas benefit and bring joy to all through the wisdom of identical essence (*samatā-jñāna*), which is precisely initial awakening (*ādikṣaya-bodhi*).
By perceiving that self and others are fundamentally non-dual and equal, they benefit and bring joy to those who see or hear them, because they take this wisdom of identical essence as the reality.
This refers to the supreme *nirmāṇa-kāya* Buddha, meaning the sovereign *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya*.
Because he manifests bodies in eight forms (*aṣṭākāra*) in accordance with time, place, and appropriate circumstances through unimpeded equanimity to transform all sentient beings;
that is to say, [the passage from] "equally seeing the Buddha" [to the end].
The commentary states: regarding the subsequent samādhi-contemplation of the Buddha, this explains that sentient beings equally see the Buddha by relying on the power of samādhi.

Because there is no distinct understanding apart from what is observed through the faculties, the appearance of the Buddhas in the world is like the hair on a horn—meaning that the horn itself is produced with its skin already formed.
Within this realm of sentient beings, it contains much hair; how much more so the bodies of the Buddhas?

This means that the Tathāgatas manifest their bodies within the realm of sentient beings throughout successive kalpas in immeasurable numbers, yet ordinary beings outside these kalpas do not perceive them.

Because one does not perceive the Buddha while practicing samādhi, it is said that from the moment the bodhicitta is generated, the Bodhisattva uses the power of samādhi to contemplate the Buddha’s Dharma-body as equal and without distinction, identical to True Suchness (*tathatā*).
One perceives only the differences between the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) and the *sambhogakāya* (enjoyment body), which exist solely within one's own faculties;
it is not because there is any differentiation in the essential nature of the Dharmatā-kāya or the true self. Therefore, it is said to be "equal."
"Having seen the Buddha...
having already entered the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
The commentary states: Regarding the subsequent section on the distinct exposition of the gates, there are two parts; first is the summary that delineates the divisions.
"What is [the meaning] up to 'because it corresponds with function'?

The commentary explains: regarding the subsequent classification of characteristics by way of the gates, there are two parts. First, the stage of the forty minds prior to entering the state of correct determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), as well as all those of the two vehicles who have not yet attained the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*);
this is because they have not yet realized the true principle of the emptiness of phenomena through the latter two wisdoms.

This is not called the "correct position" (*samyaktva-niyāma*). This clarifies that ordinary beings who are to be converted, those of the two vehicles, and the bodhisattvas of the three stages of worthiness practice according to their respective capacities through the cultivation of the mind and the cultivation of the mental consciousness;

relying solely on the power of faith, they have not yet attained fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and thus do not correspond with its essence, nor have they yet attained subsequent wisdom (*prṣṭha-labdha-jñāna*) and thus do not correspond with its function. Therefore, it was asked above regarding the stage prior to the [ten] grounds.

Question: At the stage of the forty mental states (*cittotpāda*), it is said that only the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) perfumes [the seeds]; once one has entered the stages (*bhūmi*), it is then said that the mental faculty (*manas*) perfumes them.
Why, then, is it stated here that those in the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*) perfume by means of the mental faculty? Answer: There are two interpretations. The first says:

The former statement was based on the manifest characteristics of severing the attachment to persons (*pudgala-grāha*), and thus spoke only of the mental consciousness perfuming. This present statement, however, is based on the simultaneous cultivation of suppressing the attachment to dharmas (*dharma-grāha*); therefore, it applies generally to the mental faculty.

Regarding the statement that "perfuming occurs solely in the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)," this refers specifically to the wisdom capable of severing [afflictions] at the stage prior to the Ground (*bhūmi*), which is said to perfume based on the afflictions to be severed within its own respective stage.
This refers to the wisdom of initial awakening (*ādikṣaṇabodhi*) that severs [afflictions]; it does not mean that perfuming occurs solely in the shallow and coarse mental consciousness.
In reality, it also perfumes the deep and subtle mind (*manas*). Therefore, there is no contradiction.
"What is [the process] up to the extinction of ignorance?

The commentary explains: Subsequently, bodhisattvas who have entered the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) within the ten stages obtain fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), which corresponds to the essence, and externally obtain subsequent wisdom (*pṛṣṭha-labdha-jñāna*), which corresponds to its function.
Relying on the power of the original permeation (*vāsanā*), they practice, realize suchness (*tathatā*), and sever ignorance.
Therefore, the two treatises mutually reveal that essence and function support one another; the meaning is manifest, and it is merely that the phrasing is subtle.
This concludes the section on the distinction between the exhaustive and the inexhaustible.
The commentary states: Regarding the fifth section, the distinction between the exhaustive and the inexhaustible, there are two parts; first is the summary reference.
This section [extends] to the point where the activities performed are identical.

The commentary explains that what follows correctly clarifies the two aspects; first, it interprets the gate of meaning, and third, it provides an exhaustive explanation of the distinction between the finite and the infinite.
It first states that false defilements are not consistent with the principle of reality because they have a beginning but no end, whereas all pure dharmas arise through accordance with the Path.

The principle has a beginning but no end; next, the discussion of the true and the false proceeds by way of their absolute mutual opposition, for it is a necessary principle that when defilement arises, purity is exhausted, and when purity arises, defilement is exhausted—a relationship of mutual exclusion.

Finally, the discussion of the true and the false as being without superiority or inferiority sweeps away all notions of the essence and characteristics of the true and the false, for they are equal in substance and without exhaustion.
As in the original [text] (up to) "because there is no interruption.
The commentary states that this subsequently corresponds to the first of the three meanings in the preceding section of the treatise.
From the above (up to) the three kinds of great significance.
The commentary states: Regarding the subsequent three great meanings of arising and ceasing, there are two parts.

First, this section serves as a summary that points toward the "Section on Establishing the Meaning" (*liyi-fen*), specifically the intrinsic nature, characteristics, and functions therein. Now, this treatise explicitly reveals the three kinds of great meanings within the "Gate of Arising and Ceasing" (*shengmie-men*).
The root text says: "Because of the application of meaning.
The commentary says: "The subsequent revelation has two parts; first, the recitation of the root text.
The treatise says: "[... up to "this is called the six."
The commentary states: Regarding the subsequent exposition, there are three parts. First, the headings are set forth.
Now, up to the point where it says "one should examine and discern," the commentary next points to the explanation to encourage investigation.
Furthermore, [the section] up to the two meanings of essence (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
The commentary states that there are two parts following the sequential determination; first, the extensive explanation of the three greatnesses (*mahattva*), which further divides into two.
First, the explanation of essence and characteristics, which again divides into two: first, the general indication and brief reference.
From here [to] the separate explanation and detailed exposition.
The commentary states that the subsequent separate explanation and detailed exposition has two parts, the first of which indicates the subject matter.
First, the greatness of the essence (*svabhāva-mahattva*) is explained.
The commentary states that the subsequent explanation has two parts. First, the section on the meaning of the greatness of the essential nature (*svabhāva-mahātmya*), which further has two parts.
First, the general indication: "How... because it is the single true reality.
The commentary states that the subsequent detailed explanation has two parts. First, the section on the equality of the five persons, which has three parts. First, the section explaining the meaning.

Among people there are superior and inferior, yet in truth there is neither increase nor decrease. Although the causes and effects of ordinary beings and those of limited scope differ externally in their physical forms, how could they ever be different in essence?

Therefore, the five types of persons are shown to establish a single equality; the principle that there is truly no increase or decrease is as such, and by the same logic, there should likewise be no distinction between great and small.
To weary oneself with the differences of ordinary and limited beings, and to abandon the distinct characteristics of cause and effect, is to possess the fivefold discrimination of the Real.
It is of a single taste.
Therefore, [it is said that] there is increase and decrease. The commentary states:
Next, scriptural authority is cited as proof, such as how a single vajra may take the forms of beings in the five destinies, despite differences in their superior or inferior status.
In reality, there is no difference of increase or decrease.
As in the original [text]... (up to) "...because there is increase and decrease.
The commentary states that this subsequently accords with the root treatise.
"What is [the meaning] from 'how' (yathā) to 'furthermore, because it is real'?
The commentary states: Regarding the two gates of the non-reversal of subsequent times, first is the gate of explaining the meaning. The true nature (*tathatā*) is unchanging;
the essence of awakening is concentrated and eternal, not shifting across the three periods of time. The four characteristics do not revolve—it is tranquil and yet tranquil, true and yet true.
"As in the original [text]... because it is eternal and constant.

The commentary explains: the subsequent section synthesizes with the original treatise; "neither before nor after" reveals the immovability of the three time periods; "neither arising nor ceasing" clarifies that the four characteristics do not undergo transition.
The section on the great meaning of the characteristics has already been explained.
The commentary states that there are two parts to the subsequent section on the great meaning of the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
First is the summary reference: because it is perfected and lacks nothing.
The commentary states: The subsequent exposition has three parts. First, regarding the gate of the perfection of qualities, there are two sections.
First, citing and indicating that the qualities—both named and unnamed—are complete.
What are the qualities of the nature and meaning? (From "What" to "nature and meaning" qualities).

The commentary states: Regarding the subsequent analysis of the "possessing" (*samanvāgata*), there are two parts. First, there is the title; second, the enumeration of the merits, which has four sections.
Within the first section, the original treatise explains the six divisions in three parts. First is the general inquiry and explanation: "What are the six?"
The commentary states: Next, there are three parts to the specific investigation and explanation; first is the inquiry.
[The text from] "First" [to] "the meaning of the nature of total pervasiveness" is the inquiry.
The commentary continues: Next is the explanation: first, setting aside the darkness of fundamental ignorance to establish the light of the wisdom of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*).

Second, by eliminating the delusion of ignorance regarding the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, one establishes the meaning of the original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) as the universally illuminating treasury of the *dharmadhātu*.
Third, by departing from the false measurements of conceptual construction, one establishes the meaning of the original enlightenment as true cognitive awareness.

Fourth, by departing from the dust-like burdens of artificial karma, afflictions, and deluded consciousness, one establishes the meaning of the original enlightenment as the intrinsically pure mind; this is not a matter of manifesting the self through the power of another.

Because it is the nature [of reality], it is far removed from worldly entanglements; this explains the meaning of "purity" in the preceding *Śuddhi-samādhi* (Purity Samādhi). Because it is the reality, it clarifies the meaning of the "mind.
Fifth, by departing from the four obstacles—which are like flames and illusions—these two types of awakening (*bodhi*) and the four virtues are established.

Sixth, by departing from the two kinds of birth-and-death, namely the heat of affliction and the obstruction of transformation, the two fundamental awakenings (*mūla-bodhi*) are established as cool, unchanging, and sovereign, like the north and south poles of a mirror.

The fundamental awakening that accords with and opposes defilement and purity follows whatever it is perfumed by; when defiled, it appears as defiled yet is eternally empty, like the south side of a mirror.

When facing the mirror’s surface, whatever object is set before it appears according to its substance. The pure fundamental awakening does not follow the perfuming of defiled phenomena to appear as defiled;
it is like the north side of a mirror, which, being turned away from the surface, does not manifest external objects despite their presence.
Because it is a reflection;
these are called the six. [The commentary] provides the concluding explanation at the end.
As in the original [treatise] (up to): "Because of the meaning of mastery.
The commentary explains this by joining it back to the original treatise:
"Vast" (up to): "Because of opening up the four into three."
The commentary states: Two pairs of sūtras reveal many [categories]. First, the *Pūrṇa-sūtra*; second, the *Vistara-sūtra*, which provides detailed exposition;
there is no need to cite them here in advance. Furthermore, they reveal up to eleven [categories].
The commentary states: Following the *Vimala-sūtra*, what are the distinct characteristics of these three enumerations?
The commentary states: These three collectively inquire after the three marks.
From Aśvaghoṣa [up to] the establishment of the six categories in total. The commentary states:
There are two intentions for opening and classifying the names of the four assemblies. First, the general inquiry regarding the intent of the treatise;

second, the response concerning the three numbers. Regarding the first inquiry, its intent has three aspects. By way of contrast, the latter two [sections] likewise each possess three aspects: first, to manifest the concise while possessing the extensive.

Because they are taught as dhāraṇīs in summary; because two [of them] subsume many particulars and are taught as dhāraṇīs; and because the profusion of names and characteristics might cause confusion regarding the truth.
As for the statement "seventeen," it refers to what is called the seventeen [dharmas].
The commentary states: Regarding the subsequent opening of the names of the sūtras, there are two parts.
First, the inquiry and explanation of the seventeen types [of qualities], as clearly explained from the words "twenty-five" onwards.

The commentary further states: regarding the second part, the inquiry and explanation of the twenty-five transformative virtues, these refer to all [qualities] from the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga) onwards.
All Buddhas are called the "upward-flowing" (ūrdhva-srotas), while all sentient beings who have not yet returned to the adamantine mind are called the "downward-flowing" (adhah-srotas).
This fundamental awakening (mūla-awakening) is eternally pervasive throughout cause and effect:

it does not lose its virtue of transformation and manifestation within the state of Buddhahood, nor does it lose its virtue of transformation and manifestation within the state of sentient beings. It is precisely this that constitutes the mirror of inconceivable karmic conditions and habitual perfuming.
Regarding the eightfold "virtue that is not virtue," the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:

"Neither arising nor ceasing, neither permanent nor annihilated, neither identical nor different, neither coming nor going. A detailed commentary by Yuankang is omitted here for fear of being too prolix.
The section on merits has already been explained. The commentary states:
regarding the subsequent "immeasurable merits" (*apramāṇa-guṇa*), there are two parts; first is the introductory summary.
Fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) transcends mental activity (*citta-saṃskāra*).

The commentary states that there are four subsequent sections of detailed analysis. First, a general clarification of the excessive measure has two parts. The first is "transcending words and surpassing the mind," from "By what...
up to "...the sands of the Ganges. The commentary then reconciles these numbers with the original text.
"Thus... up to ... because they are not separate.

The commentary explains that there are three distinct clarifications of these three meanings. First, regarding "not being separate," the question is posed as follows: although many distinct [phenomena] are answered, they are ultimately one mind;
though the dharmas of the single mind have two kinds of functions, they are inherently not separate from one another—that is, the mind is not separate from its qualities.
"Not separated from itself" refers to virtue; "not separated from the mind" refers to the union of these two aspects.
Because they are not separated, [the text] says "thus... until... uninterrupted.

The commentary explains: next, regarding the nature of uninterrupted virtue, because it is a wondrous existence that is never interrupted, the meritorious qualities of the pure essence are not something other.
"Because of defilement.
Thus, up to "because it is not different. The commentary states:
at the end of the word "concluding" (*zhōng*), below the character for "concluding," there is one [character] cited from the *Yùxī* (Yùxī Commentary).

The term "not" (bu) signifies that the manifest pure virtues are not distinct from the essence; because the virtues of nature are entirely the single dharma-realm, they are not separate or differentiated.
This is because there is a distinction between the immediate and the remote. Thus, [it is] inconceivable.
The commentary states: Regarding the three bases for distinguishing superiority among persons, there are two points. First, it is not the domain of others;
because the nature-virtue of these bodhisattvas is inconceivable to the minds of ordinary beings, it is severed from thought and severed from speech, being remote and utterly remote.
"Because the three [vehicles] reach the Buddha-dharma. The commentary states:
"The latter refers exclusively to the domain of the Buddha; this reveals that the nature-endowment (*prakṛti-guṇa*) follows the track of the Buddha alone.
Thus, it reaches the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*)."

The commentary states: The four [aspects] manifest the perfection of the fundamental virtues; this refers to the nature-virtues (*dharmatā-guṇa*) which, from the stage of those bound by all fetters up to the stage of Great Enlightenment, lack nothing whatsoever.

They have existed primordially from the beginningless past and do not depend on conditions for their establishment. As for the "Tathāgatagarbha" (Womb of the Tathāgata), it is named "garbha" (womb) because it is concealed and covered;
it is a designation for being in bondage, as its name is established from the stage of those bound by all fetters. It is the locus of reliance for the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya.

The term "name-body" (*nāmakāya*) refers to the designation for one who has emerged from the entanglements (*paryutthāna*); its name is established based on the stage of Great Enlightenment (*mahābodhibhūmi*).
Having already explained [the preceding], this concludes the section on the "Gate of Exegesis.
The commentary states: Next, the "Gate of Resolving Doubts through Question and Answer" has two parts; first is the section that summarizes the headings and divides the gates.
Regarding the questioner’s inquiry, "How are they contradictory?

the commentary explains that there are two sections for clarifying the characteristics based on the subsequent gate (*dvāra*). First, the brief introductory gate, which also has two parts; first, the section explaining the meaning, which further has two parts, beginning with the explanation of the intent and the raising of the inquiry.
This is what is called "therefore it is considered difficult.

The commentary explains: The subsequent citation of the text concludes the refutation. It states that within True Suchness (*tathatā*), the very essence itself is suchness, which is far removed from the three types of conceptual constructs (*prajñapti*) and is perfected with the three types of real virtues.
It is solely this single mind, free from the marks of differentiation, and possesses no further manifold characteristics of virtue.
Dazhong states that named merits are briefly said to be of six kinds, while nameless merits are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Thus, the preceding [passage] speaks of the essence being like [space], free from all marks, whereas this passage speaks of the awakened essence possessing all virtues;
if these two appear contradictory, how are they to be reconciled?
As in the original [text] (up to) "because of merit.
The commentary states that the subsequent section joins with the root treatise.
Having already explained (up to) "the second is distinct."
The commentary states that the subsequent detailed exposition of the gates has two parts. First, the section on summarizing and categorizing the gates;
this can be seen in the general explanation of their characteristics.

The commentary further states that the subsequent demonstration of characteristics according to the gates has two parts. First, the general [section], which again has two parts: first, pointing to the two gates.
Answer: [This continues] until "there is no fault of contradiction. Explanation:

The subsequent clarification of the two characteristics has two parts. First, regarding True Suchness (*tathatā*), there is a general overview. Furthermore, within this, there are two sections. First, clarifying True Suchness while dispelling obstacles:

although the Great Reality-Characteristic (*dharmatā-lakṣaṇa*) is said to be endowed with all virtues, these are virtues in relation to defilement as contrasted with arising-and-ceasing; they are based upon True Suchness.
Because the gate is unstained, that which is to be remedied does not arise; because many virtues serve as the remedy, they are but a single characteristic of equality.
From this point until "no difference from difference" [is established].
The commentary states: Subsequently, the conditions for resolving doubts arise because, through the gate of *tathatā* (suchness), one is far removed from conceptual discrimination;

since all phenomena are identical and there is no duality, [the preceding section] ends here, and from this point onward until the section on "not being identical," it should be understood accordingly.
The commentary states: Regarding the subsequent arising and ceasing, there are two general sections; this first section provides an overview.
First, from the "repeated" [passage] up to "by means of the various modes of inquiry," it is explained.
The commentary states: Regarding the subsequent explanation, there are two parts. First, the brief exposition, which is further divided into two. First, the interrogation: "Since all... and so forth.
Since the Dharma is of a single equal flavor and exists as a solitary truth without a second essence, on what basis could one establish manifold attributes?
This raises an objection from the perspective of True Suchness (tathatā) against the perspective of Arising and Ceasing (utpāda-nirodha).

From this point until the textual characteristics become visible, the commentary states that the subsequent answer has two parts. First, it establishes the gates by indicating their characteristics: the *Samsara* (Arising and Ceasing) gate is established in contrast to defilement, whereas the *Tathatā* (Suchness) gate is not established as an antidote to defilement.
This is because [Suchness] is inherently free from defilement.
"Based upon" (up to "is") constitutes the general answer.

The commentary explains that there are two parts to the subsequent interpretation of the text: first, quoting the root text to indicate the referent; second, explaining the meaning of the term "basis," which refers to ignorance (*avidyā*). "Karma" refers to the characteristic of karma;

"consciousness" refers to the evolving consciousness, the manifesting consciousness, and the discriminating consciousness of phenomena (*vastu-vijñapti-vijñāna*). "The characteristic of arising and ceasing" is the general designation according to the conventional gate.

"Indication" (*shi*) means to manifest; it is established by way of contrast with its opposite. The single character "one" (*yi*) runs through all three locations. This brief indication is now set forth;
a detailed analysis will be provided as appropriate.
This refers to the Gate of True Suchness (*tathatā-mukha*)—this is the general purport.
The commentary states that the subsequent exposition of the meaning through dialogue consists of two parts. First, the general intent is clarified by contrasting the true and the delusive:
in the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*), there are no faults consisting of the defiled dharmas to be remedied, nor are there established the sands-of-the-Ganges virtues of purity as the removers;
therefore, True Suchness has no dual nature. In this gate of Arising and Ceasing (*saṃsāra*), however, there are faults consisting of the defiled dharmas to be remedied.
Because it can counteract impurities by establishing pure virtues that exceed the sands of the Ganges, it is said that original enlightenment (mūla-awakening) possesses boundless qualities.

Next, regarding the causal conditions for [the subsequent stages], the commentary explains that the relationship between the posterior and the prior is inverted; this clarifies the causal conditions by showing how pure dharmas are established through the inversion of defilement.
The dharmas are boundless, yet briefly summarized they do not exceed two categories. First, those with names and numbers, which consist of the three dharmas based on the karmic consciousness:
namely, first, ignorance (*avidyā*); second, the phase of karma (*karma-lakṣaṇa*); and third, the various consciousnesses (*vijñapti*).

Second, those without names or numbers, which are the three characters of the phase of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-lakṣaṇa*). Since all defiled dharmas do not transcend these, the *Śāstra* uses the character "flow" (*liú*) to represent them.
The three lower readings refer to [the distinctions] by means of the basis, the karma, and the consciousness.

That they do not flow into the characteristics of arising and ceasing is because those [characteristics] are nameless and lack numerical quantity, thereby manifesting their difference from these; thus, they do not flow into them.
Due to these two defilements acting as conditions, it causes the merits to possess such numerical quantities.
The statement "it has already been explained" up to "the second" constitutes the answer.

herein, it first clarifies the fundamental substance upon which pure phenomena depend, for the principle that "all phenomena are mind-only" is the correct reasoning, and thus one excludes [the notion of] a single mind.

Since all that is external constitutes heterodox paths, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "With the exception of the true principle of the reality-mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, everything else is the work of Māra.

just as wisdom is established in contrast to ignorance, and clarity is established in contrast to darkness, this principle is extremely clear. Below are four lines [of verse].

Because it establishes the fundamental, intrinsically pure mind of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-viśuddha-citta*).

From here until the phrase "lack of mastery," the commentary explains that the sixth virtue stands in contrast [to the preceding]. Because all delusive phenomena are characterized by feverish affliction and decay, they are in reality not self-existent.
Because it establishes the original awakening (mūla-bodhi) as possessing the virtues of purity, coolness, immutability, and sovereignty;
and because, from this point until [the end], the meaning of its characteristics is manifested.
The commentary states: Regarding the "immeasurable" (apramāṇa) virtues that follow, there are two parts. First, it establishes them in contrast to the virtues that exceed the sands of the Ganges.

From this point up to "the Tathāgata-garbha," the commentary explains that the subsequent section establishes the perfection of the qualities of the result (*phala-sampad*). If it were granted that even a single moment of mind could undergo movement and transformation, then...

thus, in the state of bondage, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha*, while in the state of liberation, it is called the *dharmakāya*,

The commentary states: The analogies of the goddess Guṇadevī and the goddess Tamasā are as explained in the "Noble Practices" chapter (*Āryacaryāparivarta*) of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Wherever the goddess Guṇadevī goes with her younger sister, she brings about auspiciousness; wherever the goddess Tamasā goes with her elder sister, she brings about calamity.

These two sisters always follow one another, constantly causing benefit and harm respectively. The former is an analogy for saṃsāra, and the latter is an analogy for the natural relationship between the true and the false.
Because truth and falsehood are like light and darkness, which depend upon one another, are equal, and are never separated.

This first section provides a general overview of the Buddhas' pure vows and intentions, which are vast and boundless;

because they give rise to the five oceans by virtue of their great vows, this chapter is titled "The Inexhaustibility of Great Vows. It begins with [the vow] to manifest as many times as there are atoms in the ten directions.
1. The ocean of the cultivation of the two types of compassion; 2. The ocean of the fulfillment of causes as numerous as the atoms of the ten directions; 3.
The ocean of gathering the faculties of sentient beings as numerous as the atoms of the ten directions; 4. The ocean of establishing vast vows as numerous as the atoms of the ten directions; 5.

The commentary states: The subsequent explanation has three parts. First, having clarified the persons and dharmas who engage in the exposition of the treatise, the following section marks and explains "equality.
By means of "oneness," it dispels and reveals the equality of nature. This is marked by three types of equality: first, the equality of person and dharma;

second, the equality of essence and function; third, the equality of wisdom and principle. Regarding "the so-called Dharma-body," the following explains these three equalities: first, the equality of the Dharma and its response.

1. The transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) belongs to that person; the two types of pure principles are called the "real-real principle," while the two types of defiled and pure principles are called the "provisional-provisional principle," as both belong to that person, for there is no distinction between the identity of person and phenomena. 2.

The fundamental nature itself is the essence (*tī*), while the branches and manifestations are the function (*yòng*); essence and function are of one body and without distinction. 3. Wisdom (*jñāna*).
Because principle and substance are non-differentiated as one, the phrase "as one substance" below sweeps away that duality;
since even this "one" is non-existent, it causes all traces to be cut off. By means of this meaning below, the inherent virtues of the nature are revealed.

Because these three are equal, they are called the "three samenesses," and the character for "sameness" is the same in all three. The commentary states that the subsequent explanation has three parts. First, it clarifies the analogy through the principle:

because the nature of the *dharmakāya* is empty, it lacks a fixed form yet can manifest as all manner of forms; just as the substance of a rabbit's horn is void and thus lacks horns, yet the "good" (the potential) gives rise to various horns.
Master Zhao said: "The *dharmakāya* has no form, yet it manifests forms in response to things; *prajñā* is without knowledge, yet it illuminates in response to conditions."
Ten thousand stimuli arrive at once without his spirit being perturbed; he faces a thousand difficulties with diverse responses without his deliberation being disturbed.

His movement is like drifting clouds; his stillness is like the "valley-spirit" (the source of life). How could he harbor thoughts of self and other, or allow his emotions to be bound by activity and stillness?
Since he has no mind for activity or stillness, he likewise possesses no form for coming or going; yet in coming and going, he does not rely on form.
Therefore, there is no vessel that does not manifest form, and movement or stillness does not depend on the mind; thus, there is no stimulus that is not answered.
This is because it is said that the Dharmakāya Buddha has no other body.

The commentary states: Next, the distinction between the True Body (*dharmakāya*) and the Responsive Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is explained in two parts. First, regarding the True Body: it is the signless *dharmakāya* Tathāgata. It is neither one nor many;

it is profoundly tranquil yet not tranquil. It is beyond the reach of mind and speech; cessation and severance are both extinguished. It is solely spontaneous (*svayambhū*) because it acts spontaneously.
According to the records of the Holy Dharma, there is no character "下" (*xià*); "阿" (*ā*) signifies the Spontaneous True Buddha and the Responsive Buddha.
The Dharma-body and Wisdom-body correspond respectively to the two [preceding] natural states; thus, the subsequent inquiry, explanation, and proof may be understood as validating the preceding.
This is because [the former] has no relation to the various [phenomena] up to [the point of] "no connection."

The commentary states: Subsequently, when the signs of the sense faculties appear and the faculty of sight perceives the Buddha manifesting birth and hearing the Buddha’s teaching, one obtains benefit solely within one's own mind;
thus, there is only the reflection and no original object. This can now be understood through the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which says:
"The Buddhas have no dharma; how could the Buddha have any teaching? It is merely according to their own minds that they are said to teach such dharmas; this is the Dharmakāya."
Within the essence, there is nothing that is related [to it], because sentient beings perceive it through their own minds;

they see the inconceivable activity-phase of fundamental awakening (mūlajñāna) as it follows conditions, and they also see the mirror-body of the pure fundamental awakening of their own mind’s nature as it is perfumed by conditions.

Furthermore, they see the bodies of the responsive and transformational Buddhas within the great function of their own minds’ self-use. Therefore, it is simply that these have no relation to the Dharma-body. As it is said:

This is the *Cakrīśana-vastra*, here translated as "Jade-Luminous Radiance Robe," a robe of adornment worn by Śakra. *Kaṃsītā*.

The commentary states: Regarding the subsequent question and answer—why is it that the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) is seen based on the *vastu-vijñāna* (phenomenal consciousness), and why is the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body) seen based on the *karma-vijñāna* (karmic consciousness)?
This is intended to reveal that the *vastu-vijñāna* upon which they depend is coarse, while the *karma-vijñāna* is subtle.

When one awakens to the coarse consciousness, one perceives only the *nirmāṇakāya*, because the Buddha-body perceived therein functions in accordance with the coarse level. When one awakens to the subtle consciousness, one perceives the *saṃbhogakāya*.
